Spontaneous symmetry breaking.idea: A ground state with less symmetry than the laws; gapless Goldstone modes or, with gauge fields, massive ones

Higgs–Anderson mechanism.idea: Gauge field acquires mass by eating the Goldstone mode — the same physics in superconductors and electroweak theory

Gauge symmetry.idea: Redundancy of description that fixes the form of interactions

Discrete symmetries.idea: P, T, C and their violations constrain dynamics from nuclei to topological insulators

Group theory and representations.idea: Symmetry groups label states and organize multiplets

Renormalization group.idea: How physics changes with scale; fixed points control long-distance behavior

Universality and scaling.idea: Microscopically different systems share exponents near fixed points

Phase transitions and criticality.idea: Non-analytic change of state; fluctuations at all scales near criticality

Effective field theory.idea: Physics at one scale described without knowing the next, with controlled corrections

Mean-field and self-consistent theories.idea: Replace fluctuating neighbours by their average; exact in high dimension or large N

Density functional methods.idea: Ground-state properties from the density alone — electrons, nuclei, classical fluids

Path integrals and imaginary time.idea: Quantum amplitudes as sums over histories; Wick rotation maps QFT onto statistical mechanics

Entropy and information.idea: Entropy as missing information, from heat engines to black holes and qubits

Entanglement.idea: Correlations without a classical description; organizes many-body states and spacetime

Holography and gauge/gravity duality.idea: A gravity theory in the bulk equals a quantum field theory on the boundary

Black-hole thermodynamics.idea: Black holes have temperature and entropy; links gravity, quantum fields and thermodynamics

Analogue gravity.idea: Wave propagation in flowing media mimics curved spacetime

Quasiparticles and collective modes.idea: Interacting systems behave like gases of emergent particles

Bose–Einstein condensation and superflui.idea: Macroscopic occupation of one quantum state — cold atoms, helium, neutron stars, superconductors

Pairing and BCS physics.idea: Attractive interactions pair fermions and open a gap — metals, nuclei, neutron stars, cold atoms

Fermi surfaces and degenerate matter.idea: Pauli blocking sets the low-energy physics of electrons, nucleons and compact stars

Topological invariants.idea: Integer-valued properties robust to smooth deformation

Berry and geometric phases.idea: Holonomy of a state transported around a loop in parameter space

Topological defects.idea: Order-parameter singularities classified by homotopy — from liquid crystals to the early universe

Solitons and nonlinear waves.idea: Shape-preserving waves where nonlinearity balances dispersion

Tunnelling and instantons.idea: Classically forbidden transitions dominated by Euclidean saddle points

Anomalies.idea: A classical symmetry broken by quantization; links particle physics to topological matter

Anyons and fractional statistics.idea: Exchange statistics beyond bosons and fermions in two dimensions

Dirac, Weyl and Majorana fermions.idea: Relativistic wave equations reappear as emergent low-energy physics in solids

Confinement and chiral symmetry breaking.idea: QCD's strong coupling generates hadron masses and new phases of matter

Vacuum energy and fluctuations.idea: The quantum vacuum has structure, with measurable and cosmological consequences

Inflation and early-universe physics.idea: Field theory and statistical physics applied to the first instants
terms: phase transition in the early universe

Green's functions and propagators.idea: Response to a point source; the same object in electrostatics, QFT and many-body theory

Linear response and fluctuation–dissipat.idea: Response to a small push is fixed by equilibrium fluctuations

Dispersion relations and causality.idea: Causality makes response functions analytic, linking absorption and refraction

Scattering theory.idea: Probing structure by what comes out — from atoms to quarks to galaxies

Waves and wave equations.idea: One mathematics for sound, light, matter waves and gravitational waves

Oscillators and resonance.idea: The universal small-oscillation model and its quantum version

Variational principles.idea: Laws as extremum conditions; the action is the common language of all branches

Hamiltonian structure and phase space.idea: Phase-space geometry underlies classical, statistical and quantum dynamics

Chaos and nonlinear dynamics.idea: Deterministic unpredictability; ergodicity as the bridge to statistical mechanics

Instabilities.idea: Small perturbations that grow — fluids, plasmas, stars, lasers

Turbulence and cascades.idea: Multiscale chaotic flow in fluids, plasmas, astrophysics and wave systems

Hydrodynamics and continuum descriptions.idea: Long-wavelength dynamics of conserved densities — from water to quark–gluon plasma

Kinetic theory and transport.idea: Distribution-function dynamics between microscopic and hydrodynamic scales

Diffusion, Brownian motion and stochasti.idea: Random microscopic kicks produce universal macroscopic laws

Non-equilibrium fluctuation theorems.idea: Exact relations for driven small systems

Disorder and localization.idea: Interference in random media halts transport — electrons, light, sound, cold atoms

Glasses, spin glasses and rugged landsca.idea: Many competing minima — glasses, proteins, optimization, neural networks

Ising and lattice models.idea: Minimal models whose behavior is universal across physics and beyond

Monte Carlo and stochastic sampling.idea: Sampling replaces exact enumeration in statistical, quantum and particle physics

Tensor networks and entanglement-based n.idea: Compressing quantum states by their entanglement structure

Machine learning and physics.idea: Learning machines as statistical-physics systems, and as tools for physics

Spin and angular momentum.idea: Rotational structure and its coupling to motion and fields

Magnetism and exchange.idea: Quantum exchange produces collective magnetic order

Equations of state.idea: Pressure–density relations connect microphysics to stars, nuclei and the cosmos

Compact objects.idea: Matter at extreme density and gravity — where nuclear, particle, GR and astro meet

Nucleosynthesis.idea: How the elements formed, linking nuclear rates to stellar and cosmic histories

Neutrinos.idea: Weakly interacting probes from reactors, the Sun, supernovae and the early universe

Dark matter.idea: Unseen mass connecting cosmology, particle physics and precision detectors

Hydrostatic and virial equilibrium.idea: Balance of pressure and gravity from stars to clouds to clusters

Radiation, blackbody and radiative trans.idea: Matter–light equilibrium, from the CMB to climate

Radiation by accelerated charges.idea: One radiation formula powering light sources, astrophysical emission and diagnostics

Lasers, coherence and stimulated emissio.idea: Phase-coherent light from stimulated emission; coherence as an order parameter

Interference and diffraction.idea: Phase-sensitive superposition, used from crystallography to gravitational-wave detection

Magnetohydrodynamics, dynamos and reconn.idea: Conducting fluids carry and amplify magnetic fields — lab, solar, galactic

Plasma oscillations, screening and Landa.idea: Collective long-range Coulomb physics in plasmas, metals and quark matter

Decoherence and open quantum systems.idea: How environments make quantum systems look classical

Quantum simulation and cold atoms.idea: Engineered quantum systems emulate models from condensed matter, nuclear and high-energy physics

Precision measurement and sensing.idea: Pushing measurement to fundamental limits to test fundamental physics

Statistical inference.idea: How evidence is weighed — from discovery claims to cosmological parameters

Dimensional analysis and scaling argumen.idea: Units constrain physics before any equation is solved

Elasticity and continuum mechanics.idea: Continuum response of solids — from metals to neutron-star crusts and cells

Gravitational waves.idea: Ripples of spacetime as a new messenger

Active matter and collective behavior.idea: Energy-consuming agents form ordered, flowing phases — from bacteria to birds

Emergence.idea: The whole has laws its parts do not — the organizing theme of many-body physics

Dualities.idea: Two descriptions of one physics, often weak ↔ strong coupling

registry.name: PINNs and neural operators learn PDE solution maps
registry.summary: Physics-informed networks put the residual of the differential equation and its boundary conditions into the loss. Neural operators (DeepONet, Fourier neural operator) learn the whole solution map f↦u, a nonlinear generalization of the Green's-function integral operator, written as a kernel integral or a spectral multiplier.
registry.map: u(x)=\int G(x,x')f(x')dx'\to u=\mathcal G_\theta[f];\ \mathcal L\supset\lambda\|\mathcal N u_\theta\|^2
registry.breaks: Unlike a Green's function, the learned operator carries no guarantee of causality, conservation or accuracy outside its training distribution.
sources: Raissi, Perdikaris & Karniadakis (2019). "Physics-informed neural networks: A deep learning framework for solving forward and inverse problems involving nonlinear partial differential equations". *J. Comput. Phys.* 378, 686. [doi:10.1016/j.jcp.2018.10.045](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2018.10.045)

registry.name: Learned likelihood ratios and simulation-based inference
registry.summary: A classifier trained to separate samples from two hypotheses learns their likelihood ratio, the Neyman–Pearson optimal test statistic. Neural density estimators learn posteriors straight from simulators, so frequentist and Bayesian inference work even when the likelihood is intractable, as in collider, cosmology and gravitational-wave analyses.
sources: Carleo et al. (2019). "Machine learning and the physical sciences". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 045002. [arXiv:1903.10563](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.10563)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Equivariant networks built from group representations
registry.summary: Group-equivariant networks build symmetry into the architecture. Convolutions are generalized to E(3)/SE(3) or lattice gauge groups, and features transform in irreducible representations coupled by Clebsch–Gordan products. They are used in molecular force fields and in gauge-equivariant flows for lattice QCD, where they need far less data and keep the symmetry exact.
sources: Carleo et al. (2019). "Machine learning and the physical sciences". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 045002. [arXiv:1903.10563](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.10563)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Buckingham π as a prior for symbolic regression
registry.summary: Symbolic-regression systems that rediscover physical laws (e.g. AI Feynman) apply the π theorem first, cutting the number of independent variables before searching formula space. Surrogates fed dimensionless groups generalize across scales, the same way similarity lets wind-tunnel results transfer.
sources: Buckingham (1914). "On Physically Similar Systems; Illustrations of the Use of Dimensional Equations". *Phys. Rev.* 4, 345. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.4.345](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.4.345)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Which conservation laws an MD run actually keeps
registry.summary: Pair forces obey Newton's third law, so velocity Verlet conserves total momentum to round-off. Periodic boundaries break rotational invariance, so angular momentum is not conserved. Nosé–Hoover thermostats break energy conservation on purpose but conserve an extended Hamiltonian, and drift in any of these quantities flags a bug or too large a time step.
sources: Verlet (1967). "Computer 'Experiments' on Classical Fluids. I. Thermodynamical Properties of Lennard-Jones Molecules". *Phys. Rev.* 159, 98. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.159.98](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.159.98)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Monte Carlo as a product of Los Alamos big science
registry.summary: Ulam, von Neumann and Metropolis developed statistical sampling for neutron-transport problems at Los Alamos, and the 1953 Metropolis algorithm ran on the MANIAC computer. Simulation, a third way between theory and experiment, grew directly out of wartime big science and the first electronic computers.
sources: Metropolis et al. (1953). "Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines". *J. Chem. Phys.* 21, 1087. [doi:10.1063/1.1699114](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1699114)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Sign problem: deforming path integrals into ℂ
registry.summary: With complex weights (finite-density QCD, real-time path integrals, frustrated fermions), importance sampling breaks down. Picard–Lefschetz theory moves the integration contour onto steepest-descent thimbles where the phase is constant, and complex Langevin complexifies the fields. Both carry saddle-point methods from complex analysis into Monte Carlo.
registry.breaks: Thimbles still interfere with each other, and complex Langevin can converge to wrong answers. The general sign problem is NP-hard, so these are only partial cures.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Feynman–Kac: random walks solve diffusion-type PDEs
registry.summary: The Feynman–Kac formula writes the solution of the imaginary-time Schrödinger or diffusion equation, a Green's-function propagator, as an average over Brownian paths. Diffusion and Green's-function quantum Monte Carlo use it to project out ground states, and walk-on-spheres solves Laplace and Poisson problems.
registry.breaks: For fermions the walkers' weights change sign, so the method needs a fixed-node approximation.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: MCMC: Boltzmann samplers became posterior samplers
registry.summary: Set $E(\theta)=-\ln[L(D|\theta)\pi(\theta)]$ and $\beta=1$, and the Metropolis chain, built for Boltzmann weights, samples the Bayesian posterior. This drives cosmological and global particle-physics fits. Hybrid Monte Carlo, invented for lattice QCD, became the default sampler in Bayesian software (Stan's NUTS is a variant).
sources: Metropolis et al. (1953). "Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines". *J. Chem. Phys.* 21, 1087. [doi:10.1063/1.1699114](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1699114)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Monte Carlo propagation of distributions (GUM-S1)
registry.summary: When the measurement model is strongly nonlinear or the inputs are non-Gaussian, the first-order law of propagation fails. GUM Supplement 1 replaces it with Monte Carlo: sample the input distributions, push each sample through the model and read the coverage interval off the output distribution.

registry.name: Analytic PDE structure underpins numerical schemes
registry.summary: The same boundary- and initial-value problems are solved analytically (separation of variables, Sturm–Liouville eigenbases, Green's functions) and numerically. Spectral methods expand in those eigenfunctions, finite elements are Galerkin projections of the weak form, and well-posedness reappears as numerical stability.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Discrete Noether theorem for variational integrators
registry.summary: Integrators derived from a discrete action inherit its symmetries: a discrete Noether theorem makes them conserve the corresponding momenta exactly. Because they are symplectic, they also conserve a modified Hamiltonian over exponentially long times, so energy errors stay bounded instead of drifting.
registry.map: \tilde H=H+\Delta t^pH_{p+1}+\dots;\ |H(t)-H(0)|=O(\Delta t^p)\ \text{for}\ t\lesssim e^{c/\Delta t}
registry.breaks: Energy itself is not exactly conserved, because a fixed step breaks continuous time-translation symmetry. Adaptive step sizes destroy the symplectic guarantee.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: MPS as iterated SVD; bond dimension bounds entanglement
registry.summary: A matrix product state is built from repeated Schmidt (singular-value) decompositions of the state vector. Keeping the χ largest singular values is the optimal low-rank approximation (Eckart–Young), χ caps the bipartite entanglement, and DMRG is a Lanczos-type variational eigenproblem on this manifold.
registry.breaks: Efficient only for area-law states. Volume-law states, such as those after long quenches, need χ exponential in system size.
sources: White (1992). "Density matrix formulation for quantum renormalization groups". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 69, 2863. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.2863](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.2863)
Schollwöck (2011). "The density-matrix renormalization group in the age of matrix product states". *Ann. Phys.* 326, 96. [arXiv:1008.3477](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.3477)

registry.name: Broken symmetry as the paradigm of emergence
registry.summary: Anderson's 'More is different' uses spontaneous symmetry breaking as its central example of emergence: a ground state can lack the symmetry of the laws, and rigidity, order parameters and Goldstone modes follow. Philosophers debate whether this is genuine emergence, because strict SSB needs the infinite-volume limit.
sources: Anderson (1972). "More Is Different". *Science* 177, 393. [doi:10.1126/science.177.4047.393](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.177.4047.393)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: SSB migrated from superconductivity to particle physics
registry.summary: Nambu (1960–61) took the BCS ground state and the puzzle of its gauge invariance as the template for spontaneously broken symmetry in particle physics, and Goldstone generalized the massless mode. Anderson (1963) and Englert–Brout, Higgs and Guralnik–Hagen–Kibble (1964) then showed how gauge fields evade it, a textbook case of an idea crossing from condensed matter.
sources: Nambu (1960). "Quasi-Particles and Gauge Invariance in the Theory of Superconductivity". *Phys. Rev.* 117, 648. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.117.648](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.117.648)
Goldstone (1961). "Field theories with Superconductor solutions". *Nuovo Cimento* 19, 154. [doi:10.1007/BF02812722](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02812722)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Gleason and Kochen–Specker: Born rule and contextuality
registry.summary: Two interpretive questions are settled as theorems about Hilbert space. Gleason: for dim ≥ 3, every additive probability measure on projectors has the form Tr(ρP), so the Born rule follows from the lattice of subspaces. Kochen–Specker: no noncontextual assignment of definite values to all projectors exists, which constrains hidden-variable interpretations.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Hole argument: diffeomorphisms and gauge redundancy
registry.summary: General covariance makes a metric and its pullback by a diffeomorphism physically equivalent. Einstein's hole argument turns this into the substantivalism–relationism debate, settled in practice by treating only diffeomorphism-invariant quantities as observable. The fibre-bundle view of gauge fields gets the same reading: only holonomies and curvature are physical ('gauge as redundancy').
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Arrow of time vs. microscopic T violation
registry.summary: The fundamental laws are T-invariant except for the weak interaction, where CP violation together with CPT implies T violation. Philosophers of physics stress that this small, Hamiltonian-level asymmetry does not explain the thermodynamic arrow, which instead traces to a low-entropy initial state (the past hypothesis).
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Are c, ħ, G fundamental or just unit conversions?
registry.summary: Natural units set c, ħ, G and k_B to 1, which shows that dimensionful constants act largely as unit conversions. Only dimensionless combinations such as α or m_p/m_e are unit-independent and can be meaningfully tested for variation. How many dimensionful constants are fundamental (three, two or none) is still debated, notably in the Duff–Okun–Veneziano 'trialogue'.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Point vs. set paradigms of measurement in learning
registry.summary: PER finds that many students treat a single reading as 'the true value' (point paradigm) instead of seeing a measurement as a distribution summarized by a best estimate and an uncertainty (set paradigm). Lab curricula built on the GUM framework target this shift, so uncertainty is both a metrology topic and a documented learning difficulty.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Symmetry acts through linear representations
registry.summary: Symmetry groups act on state spaces through linear, usually unitary or projective, representations. Group theory in physics therefore runs on the mathematical-methods toolkit: Hilbert-space operators and eigenproblems, special functions as representation bases, and differential geometry for Lie groups and gauge connections.
sources: Wigner (1939). "On Unitary Representations of the Inhomogeneous Lorentz Group". *Ann. Math.* 40, 149. [doi:10.2307/1968551](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968551)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Causal transfer functions: Kramers–Kronig, Bode, Nyquist
registry.summary: A causal, stable signal chain has a transfer function analytic in a half-plane, so its gain and phase are tied together (Kramers–Kronig, Bode). The Nyquist criterion, the argument principle applied to the loop gain, decides whether a feedback amplifier or phase-locked loop oscillates. Bode's relations limit how much feedback a front end can have over a given bandwidth.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Special functions as representation matrix elements
registry.summary: The classical special functions are matrix elements or bases of Lie-group representations: spherical harmonics and Legendre polynomials for SO(3), Wigner D-functions for SU(2), Bessel functions for the Euclidean group E(2), Hermite functions for the Heisenberg–Weyl group. Their addition theorems, recursions and orthogonality follow from group multiplication, ladder operators and Peter–Weyl.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Lie groups were invented to integrate ODEs
registry.summary: Sophus Lie built the theory of continuous groups in the 1870s to do for differential equations what Galois theory did for polynomials. Each one-parameter point symmetry lowers an ODE's order by one, and symmetry reductions of PDEs give similarity solutions and separable coordinates. The algebraic core of that programme became the Lie theory physics uses today.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Self-similar solutions: scaling turns PDEs into ODEs
registry.summary: When a problem has no intrinsic scale, dimensional analysis forces a similarity form that reduces the PDE to an ODE: the heat kernel, the Blasius boundary layer, the Taylor–Sedov blast wave. In second-kind (intermediate) asymptotics the exponents are not fixed by dimensions and come out as eigenvalues of the reduced problem.
sources: Buckingham (1914). "On Physically Similar Systems; Illustrations of the Use of Dimensional Equations". *Phys. Rev.* 4, 345. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.4.345](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.4.345)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Wigner's theorem: time reversal is antiunitary
registry.summary: By Wigner's theorem every quantum symmetry is unitary or antiunitary, and time reversal must be antiunitary, T=UK. For half-integer spin T²=−1, so ψ and Tψ are orthogonal with equal energy, and every level of a T-invariant Hamiltonian is at least doubly degenerate (Kramers). The same antiunitary structure fixes the random-matrix and topological symmetry classes.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Schur's lemma: symmetry dictates degeneracy
registry.summary: By Schur's lemma, an operator that commutes with an irreducible representation is a multiple of the identity on it. Symmetry-protected degeneracies therefore equal irrep dimensions (2l+1 for SO(3)) and eigenbases are labelled by Casimirs. The Wigner–Eckart theorem reduces tensor-operator matrix elements to Clebsch–Gordan coefficients, which gives the selection rules.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Gauge fields are Lie-algebra-valued connections
registry.summary: A Lie group is a manifold whose tangent space at the identity is its Lie algebra. A gauge potential is a Lie-algebra-valued connection one-form on a principal G-bundle, and the field strength is its curvature. Yang–Mills theory and gravity therefore share connections, parallel transport and curvature (holonomy = Wilson loop).

registry.name: Killing vectors turn ∇·T=0 into conserved charges
registry.summary: In curved spacetime, ∇_μT^{μν}=0 gives no integral conservation law by itself. Only an isometry (a Killing vector ξ) makes J^μ=T^{μν}ξ_ν a conserved current with a global charge, which is Noether's theorem in geometric form. The contracted Bianchi identity is the identity Noether's second theorem attaches to diffeomorphism invariance, which resolved Hilbert and Klein's 1918 energy puzzle.

registry.name: Metrology: value × unit ± uncertainty, traceable to SI
registry.summary: A complete measurement result is a number times an SI unit plus an uncertainty. Traceability links any instrument through an unbroken calibration chain to the unit definitions, and since the 2019 redefinition that chain ends at exact constants rather than artefacts.
sources: Stock et al. (2019). "The revision of the SI—the result of three decades of progress in metrology". *Metrologia* 56, 022001. [doi:10.1088/1681-7575/ab0013](https://doi.org/10.1088/1681-7575/ab0013)

registry.name: EDM and CPT tests as noise-limited precision measurements
registry.summary: Two kinds of experiment are limited by sensor noise: searches for permanent electric dipole moments (the neutron, the electron in polar molecules), which would violate P and T, and CPT tests comparing particles with antiparticles in Penning traps or by antihydrogen spectroscopy. Their reach on new CP violation is set by magnetometry, spin-precession readout and cryogenic trap techniques.

registry.name: Josephson and QHE standards realize volt, ohm, kilogram
registry.summary: Quantum electrical devices turn the exact h and e into units: Josephson arrays give voltages nf/K_J and quantum Hall bars give resistances R_K/i. The Kibble balance balances mechanical against electrical power measured with both, which realizes the 2019 kilogram from h.

registry.name: CODATA adjustment as generalized least squares
registry.summary: CODATA recommended values come from a linearized generalized least-squares fit of well over a hundred correlated experimental and theoretical inputs. Consistency is checked with the Birge ratio and normalized residuals, and discrepant inputs get expanded uncertainties. The roughly 5σ disagreement between the Cs and Rb atom-recoil values of α is the kind of tension this step has to absorb.

registry.name: Unit realizations carry GUM uncertainty budgets
registry.summary: Each realization of an SI unit reports a GUM budget of Type A and Type B components: the Kibble balance or silicon-sphere XRCD for the kilogram, acoustic-gas or Johnson-noise thermometry for the kelvin. Traceability carries that uncertainty down the calibration chain into every measurement.

registry.name: Lyapunov instability underlies MD ergodicity
registry.summary: Many-particle MD trajectories are chaotic with positive Lyapunov exponents, so individual trajectories are irreproducible after picoseconds while time averages converge to ensemble averages; chaos is what makes MD statistics robust.

registry.name: Hamiltonian (hybrid) Monte Carlo
registry.summary: HMC proposes moves by integrating fictitious Hamiltonian dynamics with leapfrog; time reversibility and Liouville volume preservation make the Metropolis correction exact.

registry.name: Symplectic integrators ↔ Hamiltonian flow
registry.summary: Leapfrog/Verlet and other symplectic schemes are exact flows of a nearby 'shadow' Hamiltonian, so they preserve phase-space volume and show no secular energy drift; the integrator inherits the symplectic structure of Hamilton's equations.
registry.breaks: Backward-error bound holds only for fixed step size; adaptive steps or dissipation destroy the shadow Hamiltonian.

registry.name: Variational integrators and Ritz–Galerkin
registry.summary: Discretizing the action rather than the equations gives variational integrators that are automatically symplectic and momentum-conserving (discrete Noether); finite elements are Ritz minimization of an energy functional.

registry.name: Finite elements born in structural elasticity
registry.summary: The finite element method grew out of structural and elasticity analysis (Courant's 1943 variational triangles, 1950s aircraft stress analysis) and is a Ritz–Galerkin minimization of the elastic energy.

registry.name: DNS and spectral solvers ↔ turbulence
registry.summary: Direct numerical simulation must resolve from the integral scale L down to the Kolmogorov scale η, so grid points grow as Re^{9/4}; pseudospectral FFT methods and LES closures are the workhorses of turbulence research.

registry.name: N-body integrators ↔ celestial mechanics
registry.summary: Long-term Solar System integrations use symplectic map methods (Wisdom–Holman splitting into Kepler drift plus interaction kick) and regularization for close encounters.

registry.name: Lyapunov spectra and shadowing in numerics
registry.summary: Lyapunov exponents are computed by tangent-map integration with repeated QR (Gram–Schmidt) reorthonormalization; the shadowing lemma justifies trusting chaotic numerical orbits statistically even though each diverges from the true one.

registry.name: Standard map = leapfrog kicked rotor
registry.summary: Chirikov's standard map is the symplectic-Euler discretization of a pendulum and the exact flow of the kicked rotor; KAM theory explains why symplectic integrators keep invariant tori and stay stable for exponentially long times.

registry.name: Rutherford scattering discovered the nucleus
registry.summary: Rutherford's classical Coulomb-orbit cross-section, fitted to Geiger–Marsden α data, revealed the atomic nucleus; the same formula happens to be exact in quantum mechanics.

registry.name: Liouville, recurrence and the arrow of time
registry.summary: Time-reversal-invariant Hamiltonian flow preserves phase-space volume, so fine-grained Gibbs entropy is constant and Poincaré recurrence holds; irreversibility needs coarse-graining plus a low-entropy past.

registry.name: Conformal maps for 2D potential flow and lift
registry.summary: Planar irrotational incompressible flow is an analytic complex potential; Joukowski conformal maps generate airfoils and the Blasius contour integral gives the Kutta–Joukowski lift.

registry.name: Small divisors and analytic estimates in KAM
registry.summary: Lindstedt perturbation series diverge because of small denominators k·ω; KAM proves torus survival for Diophantine frequencies by Newton iteration with Cauchy estimates on shrinking complex analyticity strips.

registry.name: Inverse scattering via analytic scattering data
registry.summary: The inverse scattering transform solves KdV and NLS by mapping initial data to scattering data analytic in the spectral parameter, reconstructed through a Riemann–Hilbert (Gelfand–Levitan) problem; solitons are bound-state poles.

registry.name: Damped oscillator response ↔ causality and Kramers–Kronig
registry.summary: The driven damped oscillator's susceptibility has poles only in the lower half ω-plane because the response is causal, so its real and imaginary parts obey Kramers–Kronig; its impulse response is the retarded Green's function.

registry.name: Hamilton–Jacobi PDE ↔ method of characteristics
registry.summary: The Hamilton–Jacobi equation is a first-order nonlinear PDE whose characteristics are exactly Hamilton's equations; complete integrals give generating functions of canonical transformations.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Stokeslet = Green's function of Stokes flow
registry.summary: The Oseen tensor (Stokeslet) is the Green's function of the Stokes equations; boundary-integral, slender-body and hydrodynamic-interaction methods superpose it.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Acoustic waves ↔ retarded Green's function
registry.summary: Sound radiated by sources is the source convolved with the retarded Green's function of the wave equation; Huygens' sharp-front principle holds in odd spatial dimensions.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Floquet theory of the Mathieu equation
registry.summary: Parametric resonance is governed by Floquet–Hill theory of linear ODEs with periodic coefficients; Mathieu characteristic exponents define the instability tongues near ω = 2ω₀/n.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Poisson brackets ↔ commutators; Koopman–von Neumann
registry.summary: Dirac's rule {f,g} → [f̂,ĝ]/iħ maps Hamiltonian mechanics onto Hilbert-space operators; conversely Koopman–von Neumann write classical mechanics as unitary evolution on L²(phase space).
registry.breaks: Groenewold–van Hove: no quantization map preserves all brackets beyond quadratic polynomials.

registry.name: Normal modes = generalized eigenproblem
registry.summary: Small oscillations about equilibrium reduce to the symmetric generalized eigenproblem Kv = ω²Mv; normal modes are the orthogonal eigenvectors guaranteed by the spectral theorem.

registry.name: Principal axes = spectral theorem for the inertia tensor
registry.summary: The inertia tensor is real symmetric, so it has orthogonal eigenvectors (principal axes) and real eigenvalues (principal moments); rotational kinetic energy is diagonal in that basis.

registry.name: Phase space as a symplectic manifold
registry.summary: Phase space is the cotangent bundle T*Q with symplectic 2-form ω = dp∧dq; Hamilton's equations are ι_X ω = dH, Poisson brackets come from ω^{-1}, and Liouville's theorem is conservation of the volume form ω^n.

registry.name: Strain compatibility = flat metric; defects = torsion and curvature
registry.summary: Saint-Venant compatibility is the vanishing Riemann tensor of the deformed metric g = δ + 2ε; in the geometric theory of defects dislocations are torsion and disclinations curvature of a material connection.

registry.name: Fictitious forces as connection coefficients
registry.summary: Coriolis and centrifugal forces are the Christoffel symbols of rotating coordinates in flat space; writing Newton's law covariantly prefigures the equivalence principle.

registry.name: Resonant sensors: Q, bandwidth and thermal force noise
registry.summary: Mechanical and electrical resonators used as sensors are driven damped oscillators; Q sets the bandwidth f₀/Q and the lock-in readout, and via fluctuation–dissipation the thermal force-noise floor.

registry.name: Least squares born from orbit determination
registry.summary: Gauss developed least squares and the normal error law to recover the orbit of Ceres (1801–1809); χ² fitting of orbital elements remains the template for parameter estimation.

registry.name: Kepler's hidden SO(4) and the Runge–Lenz vector
registry.summary: The conserved Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector together with L generates SO(4) for bound Kepler orbits, explaining closed ellipses (Bertrand) and, once quantized, the n² degeneracy of hydrogen (Pauli 1926).

registry.name: KdV hierarchies ↔ infinite-dimensional Lie algebras
registry.summary: Integrable soliton equations come in hierarchies attached to Kac–Moody algebras (Drinfeld–Sokolov); the Lax pair is a flat connection in a loop algebra and tau functions carry representations of infinite-dimensional groups.

registry.name: Rotation group SO(3) ↔ rigid-body motion
registry.summary: A rigid body's configuration space is SO(3); Euler's equations are the Lie–Poisson equations on so(3)*, and the inertia tensor defines a left-invariant metric whose geodesics are torque-free motions.

registry.name: Invariance of the action → Noether currents
registry.summary: Noether's theorem is a statement about the variational principle: a continuous transformation leaving the action invariant up to a boundary term yields a conserved quantity; cyclic coordinates are the simplest case.
registry.map: \delta L=\frac{dK}{dt}\Rightarrow Q=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}\delta q-K,\ \dot Q=0

registry.name: Kelvin circulation from particle-relabelling symmetry
registry.summary: In the Lagrangian (Euler–Poincaré) formulation of ideal fluids, invariance under relabelling of fluid particles is a Noether symmetry whose charge is circulation; Kelvin's theorem and potential-vorticity conservation follow.
registry.breaks: Exact only for ideal barotropic fluids; viscosity and baroclinic torques break it.

registry.name: Newtonian mechanics as symmetry consequences
registry.summary: The Galilean symmetry group of Newtonian mechanics (translations, rotations, boosts) fixes its conserved quantities; the Galilean boost charge gives uniform centre-of-mass motion.
sources: Noether (1918; English translation 1971). "Invariant variation problems". *Transport Theory Stat. Phys.* 1, 186. [doi:10.1080/00411457108231446](https://doi.org/10.1080/00411457108231446)

registry.name: Noether's theorem ↔ energy, momentum, angular momentum
registry.summary: The conservation laws of Newtonian mechanics are the Noether charges of time translation, space translation and rotation invariance of the action.
registry.map: \partial L/\partial t=0\Rightarrow E=\dot q\,\partial L/\partial\dot q-L\ \text{conserved}
sources: Noether (1918; English translation 1971). "Invariant variation problems". *Transport Theory Stat. Phys.* 1, 186. [doi:10.1080/00411457108231446](https://doi.org/10.1080/00411457108231446)

registry.name: Integrability = enough conserved charges in involution
registry.summary: Liouville–Arnold integrability needs n Poisson-commuting conserved quantities; KdV has infinitely many, generated by commuting symmetry flows, which is why solitons survive collisions.

registry.name: Elasticity as the Goldstone theory of broken translations
registry.summary: A crystal breaks continuous translations; continuum elasticity is the effective theory of the corresponding Goldstone fields (displacements), and its sound waves are the Goldstone modes.
registry.breaks: Broken rotations give no independent Goldstone modes (inverse Higgs); amorphous solids are elastic without long-range order.

registry.name: Pitchfork bifurcation = Landau symmetry breaking
registry.summary: The normal form of a Z2-symmetric pitchfork is gradient flow on a φ⁴ potential; the supercritical branch is mean-field spontaneous symmetry breaking with exponent 1/2.
registry.breaks: No fluctuations or thermodynamic limit, so only mean-field exponents; Hopf bifurcations break time translation rather than an internal symmetry.

registry.name: Kuramoto sync and Turing patterns as symmetry breaking
registry.summary: Kuramoto synchronization is a U(1)-breaking transition with order parameter re^{iψ} and mean-field exponent 1/2; Turing patterns spontaneously break translation symmetry.
registry.breaks: Driven-dissipative attractors with no free energy or detailed balance; the phase mode diffuses rather than propagating, and noise can restore the symmetry.

registry.name: Galileo's square–cube law
registry.summary: Galileo's 1638 argument that beam strength scales as L² while weight scales as L³ is the first scaling law and limits the size of animals and structures; Euler buckling follows the same logic.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Buckingham π ↔ Reynolds similarity
registry.summary: Dimensional analysis reduces drag and flow problems to functions of a few dimensionless groups (Re, Ma, Fr), which is the basis of wind-tunnel scaling and dynamic similarity.
sources: Buckingham (1914). "On Physically Similar Systems; Illustrations of the Use of Dimensional Equations". *Phys. Rev.* 4, 345. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.4.345](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.4.345)

registry.name: Re ≪ 1 regime and the scallop theorem
registry.summary: At Re ≪ 1 inertia drops out and Stokes flow is linear and instantaneous, so reciprocal strokes give no net swimming (Purcell's scallop theorem); scaling arguments set what microswimmers can do.
sources: Purcell (1977). "Life at low Reynolds number". *Am. J. Phys.* 45, 3. [doi:10.1119/1.10903](https://doi.org/10.1119/1.10903)

registry.name: Kolmogorov 1941 from dimensional analysis
registry.summary: If the inertial range depends only on the dissipation rate ε and wavenumber k, dimensional analysis fixes the −5/3 spectrum and the Kolmogorov scale; intermittency corrections are the anomalous part beyond dimensional reasoning.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Photonic neural-network hardware and ML inverse design
registry.summary: Any N×N unitary factorizes into a mesh of Mach–Zehnder interferometers (Reck and Clements decompositions). Programmable silicon-photonic meshes can therefore perform the matrix–vector products of neural-network inference optically. In the other direction, adjoint-gradient and neural-network inverse design produce non-intuitive waveguide, coupler and metasurface geometries.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Ewald summation: electrostatics on a periodic lattice
registry.summary: Periodic simulations need the Coulomb energy of an infinite lattice of images, a conditionally convergent sum. Ewald splits 1/r into a short-range erfc part summed in real space and a smooth part summed in Fourier space. The leftover surface-dipole term depends on the dielectric condition at infinity; tin-foil boundaries (ε'=∞) are the usual choice.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Monte Carlo radiative transfer through turbid media
registry.summary: Multiple scattering of light in clouds, tissue and dust is simulated as random walks of photon packets. Free paths are drawn from the extinction coefficient and scattering angles from a Mie or Henyey–Greenstein phase function. This solves the radiative transfer equation statistically where the diffusion approximation fails.
sources: Mie (1908). "Beiträge zur Optik trüber Medien, speziell kolloidaler Metallösungen". *Ann. Phys.* 330, 377. [doi:10.1002/andp.19083300302](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19083300302)

registry.name: Yee's FDTD scheme for Maxwell's curl equations
registry.summary: The finite-difference time-domain method staggers E and H by half a cell in space and half a step in time (leapfrog). The discrete curls then conserve the discrete divergence of B exactly, and of D given charge conservation, a discrete-exterior-calculus structure. Stability obeys the CFL bound. FDTD and edge-element finite elements are the workhorses of photonics and antenna design.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Split-step Fourier solution of the fibre NLSE
registry.summary: Pulse propagation in a Kerr fibre obeys the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, solved by operator splitting. Dispersion is applied exactly in the Fourier domain and self-phase modulation in the time domain; Strang splitting makes the scheme second order. This norm-preserving pseudospectral method also underlies Lugiato–Lefever simulations of Kerr combs and solitons.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Maxwell's unification and the speed of light
registry.summary: With the displacement current, Maxwell (1865) derived transverse waves travelling at 1/√(ε₀μ₀). That speed matched both Weber and Kohlrausch's measured ratio of electromagnetic to electrostatic units and the speed of light, so light became an electromagnetic wave. Hertz's 1887–88 experiments confirmed it, making this the archetype of unification in physics.
sources: Maxwell (1865). "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 155, 459. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1865.0008](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1865.0008)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Electrodynamics of moving bodies gave special relativity
registry.summary: Einstein's 1905 paper opens with the magnet–conductor asymmetry of Maxwell–Lorentz electrodynamics. He resolved it by making the Lorentz transformations, which already leave Maxwell's equations invariant, the kinematics of space and time. Minkowski's 1908 tensor form then made E and B frame-dependent parts of one object, so relativity grew out of electrodynamics rather than mechanics.
sources: Einstein (1905). "Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper". *Ann. Phys.* 322, 891. [doi:10.1002/andp.19053221004](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19053221004)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Are potentials real? Gauge and the Aharonov–Bohm effect
registry.summary: The Aharonov–Bohm phase shows that charged quanta respond to A where B vanishes. This forces a choice: gauge-dependent potentials acting locally, gauge-invariant loop holonomies acting nonlocally, or nonlocal field interactions. It is the main test case for whether gauge symmetry is mere redundancy of description or physically significant.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Radiation reaction and consistency of classical ED
registry.summary: The Abraham–Lorentz–Dirac equation for a radiating point charge is third order, with runaway solutions and pre-acceleration, and the point charge's self-energy diverges. Whether classical electrodynamics of point particles is even consistent, and how to read the reduced-order Landau–Lifshitz fix, is debated in philosophy of physics. Strong-field laser experiments now probe the same question.
sources: Dirac (1938). "Classical theory of radiating electrons". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 167, 148. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1938.0124](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1938.0124)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Rays as the stationary-phase limit; Airy caustics
registry.summary: Geometric optics is the stationary-phase asymptotics of the diffraction integral as k→∞: rays are the stationary points of the optical path. Where two rays merge, the method fails at a caustic. The intensity there follows the Airy function, as in Airy's rainbow theory, which is where catastrophe optics begins.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Conformal mapping for 2D electrostatics
registry.summary: In two dimensions the potential is the real part of an analytic complex potential w(z), whose level curves are equipotentials and field lines. Conformal maps, including Schwarz–Christoffel, carry a solved geometry into edges, slots and fringing-field capacitors. It is the same tool used for 2D potential flow.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Kramers–Kronig: causality makes ε(ω) analytic
registry.summary: Polarization cannot come before the field that causes it, so the susceptibility is analytic in the upper half ω-plane. The dispersive and absorptive parts of ε(ω) are then Hilbert transforms of each other. Lorentz-oscillator models satisfy this; conductors need the DC-conductivity pole treated separately. Kronig (1926) and Kramers (1927) first derived the relations for the dispersion of light and X-rays.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Legendre generating function is the multipole expansion
registry.summary: Expanding the Coulomb kernel 1/|r−r'| in powers of r_</r_> generates the Legendre polynomials, and the addition theorem turns them into spherical harmonics. Multipole moments are just the source's expansion coefficients in these eigenfunctions of the angular Laplacian.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Huygens–Fresnel principle as a Green's-function integral
registry.summary: Kirchhoff diffraction comes from applying Green's theorem to the Helmholtz equation with the outgoing Green's function e^{ikr}/r. This turns Huygens' secondary wavelets into an exact representation. Kirchhoff's boundary conditions are inconsistent, which the Rayleigh–Sommerfeld Dirichlet Green's function repairs. Fresnel and Fraunhofer diffraction are its paraxial and far-field limits.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Waveguide and cavity modes as Sturm–Liouville eigenproblems
registry.summary: In a hollow metal guide the longitudinal field obeys the transverse Helmholtz equation, with Dirichlet conditions for TM modes (E_z=0) and Neumann conditions for TE modes (∂_nH_z=0). The eigenvalues set the cutoff frequencies. The complete orthogonal eigenfunctions are the modes into which any guided field expands, like a drum head.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Retarded potentials from the wave-equation Green's function
registry.summary: In Lorenz gauge each potential obeys a sourced wave equation, so V and A are ρ and J convolved with the retarded Green's function of the d'Alembertian. Causality selects G_ret over G_adv. Coulomb gauge trades this for an instantaneous Poisson Green's function for V.
registry.map: \Box A^\mu=\mu_0J^\mu,\ G_{\rm ret}=\frac{\delta(t-t'-|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|/c)}{4\pi|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Statics as Poisson problems for V and A
registry.summary: Electrostatics, and magnetostatics in Coulomb gauge, both reduce to Poisson equations: one for V and one for each Cartesian component of A. Coulomb's law and the Biot–Savart law are therefore both the sources convolved with the same Green's function 1/(4πr).
registry.map: \nabla^2V=-\rho/\epsilon_0,\ \nabla^2\mathbf A=-\mu_0\mathbf J\Rightarrow\mathbf A=\mu_0\int G\,\mathbf J\,d^3r',\ G=\frac{1}{4\pi|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}

registry.name: Coulomb potential as the Laplacian's Green's function
registry.summary: The point-charge potential is the free-space Green's function of the Laplacian. Dirichlet and Neumann Green's functions, the method of images and separation of variables (via Sturm–Liouville completeness) are the general PDE tools applied to conductors. Uniqueness follows from the elliptic type of the problem.

registry.name: Liénard–Wiechert fields and Dirac's radiation reaction
registry.summary: Evaluating the retarded Green's function on a point charge's worldline gives the Liénard–Wiechert potentials; the 1−n̂·β factor is the Jacobian of the retarded-time delta function. Dirac took the radiation-reaction field to be half the retarded minus half the advanced field, a combination that is regular at the charge.

registry.name: Jones calculus and the polarization coherency matrix
registry.summary: Fully polarized light is a vector in C², and optical elements are 2×2 complex matrices that compose by multiplication. Partially polarized light is described by the Hermitian positive coherency matrix, which is mathematically a qubit density matrix, with the degree of polarization playing the role of purity. Birefringent principal axes are the eigenvectors of the symmetric dielectric tensor.

registry.name: Photonic bands as a Hermitian eigenvalue problem
registry.summary: For lossless periodic dielectrics the master equation for H is a Hermitian eigenproblem, so frequencies are real, modes are orthogonal and a variational principle holds. Bloch's theorem then gives photonic bands and gaps, the same spectral theory as electrons in crystals. Unlike the electron case it acts on a transverse vector field with no intrinsic length scale, so scaling a crystal by s scales its frequencies by 1/s.

registry.name: The vector potential as a U(1) connection
registry.summary: The gauge potential is a connection on a U(1) bundle and F is its curvature. Gauge transformations are changes of local section, and the Aharonov–Bohm phase is the connection's holonomy around a loop. A Dirac monopole is a topologically nontrivial bundle that needs two patches (Wu–Yang), and consistency between the patches quantizes charge.

registry.name: Maxwell's equations as dF=0 and d⋆F=J
registry.summary: In differential-form language the field strength is the exact 2-form F=dA. The homogeneous Maxwell equations are the Bianchi identity dF=0, and the sourced ones are d⋆F=⋆J. The integral laws are Stokes' theorem, the metric enters only through the Hodge star, and charge conservation follows from d²=0.

registry.name: Transformation optics: geometry as an effective medium
registry.summary: Maxwell's equations keep their form under any coordinate map if ε and μ are replaced by transformed tensors. A desired ray geometry, such as a cloak or a concentrator, is therefore designed as a coordinate transformation and built from anisotropic metamaterials. Equivalently, rays follow geodesics of an optical metric (Fermat's principle), the same mathematics that lets a medium mimic curved spacetime.
registry.breaks: Ideal cloaks need singular, impedance-matched and strongly dispersive ε and μ, so causality and losses confine real devices to narrow bands or ray-only (carpet) versions.

registry.name: Johnson–Nyquist noise and antenna temperature
registry.summary: A matched single-mode antenna inside a blackbody enclosure delivers k_BTΔf to its load. That is exactly the available Johnson–Nyquist noise of a resistor at temperature T; Nyquist himself derived it from a transmission line in equilibrium. Radio astronomers therefore quote received power as an antenna or brightness temperature, with the radiation resistance acting as a resistor whose noise is the sky.

registry.name: Super-resolution localization as parameter estimation
registry.summary: PALM and STORM beat the diffraction limit through statistics rather than better optics. Isolated emitters are fitted by maximum likelihood, and the Cramér–Rao bound puts localization precision at about the PSF width divided by √N photons. Fisher-information analysis also shows that intensity imaging loses the ability to resolve two incoherent points as they merge ('Rayleigh's curse'), which mode-sorting measurements avoid.

registry.name: Faraday rotation (T-odd) vs optical activity (P-odd)
registry.summary: Both effects rotate linear polarization. Natural optical activity comes from chirality (broken parity) and is reciprocal, so it undoes itself on retro-reflection. Faraday rotation is driven by the T-odd magnetic field and is nonreciprocal, so it doubles on the return pass. This symmetry difference is why optical isolators need magneto-optics.

registry.name: Inversion symmetry forbids second-order nonlinearity
registry.summary: Under parity both P and E change sign, so every even-order susceptibility vanishes in a centrosymmetric medium. Second-harmonic generation therefore needs non-centrosymmetric crystals, such as the quartz in Franken's experiment or LiNbO₃. SHG is used as a probe of broken inversion at surfaces, at interfaces and in ferroelectric order.

registry.name: T-breaking and absent Kramers protection for photons
registry.summary: Photonic Chern insulators with one-way edge modes need broken time reversal, from gyromagnetic or time-modulated media. Photonic 'quantum spin Hall' analogues instead use engineered pseudo-spins, which symmetry-breaking defects can couple.

The 2-to-1 homomorphism maps this to SO(3) rotations of the Stokes vector on the Poincaré sphere, the same structure as spin-½ on the Bloch sphere. A closed loop on the sphere gives the Pancharatnam geometric phase, equal to half the enclosed solid angle.

Its two invariants are E²−c²B² and E·B. In Wigner's classification the photon is the massless helicity ±1 representation of the Poincaré group.

registry.name: Multipole moments as irreducible SO(3) tensors
registry.summary: The 2l+1 spherical moments of order l form an irreducible representation of the rotation group, so a rank-l Cartesian moment reduces to its symmetric traceless part. The Wigner–Eckart theorem then gives the selection rules for multipole radiation. It also forbids moments of order l>2j in a state of angular momentum j, so a spin-½ particle has no quadrupole moment.

registry.name: Spin and orbital angular momentum of light
registry.summary: Rotational invariance gives the electromagnetic field a conserved angular momentum. For paraxial beams it splits into a spin part fixed by circular polarization (±ħ per photon, seen as torque on a wave plate by Beth in 1936) and an orbital part from helical phase fronts (ℓħ in Laguerre–Gauss beams). For general fields the split is gauge-sensitive and still debated.

registry.name: Conservation laws of electrodynamics as Noether currents
registry.summary: The continuity equation is the Noether current of the U(1) phase symmetry of charged matter. Poynting's theorem and the Maxwell stress tensor are components of the field's (Belinfante-symmetrized) energy–momentum tensor, which comes from spacetime translations. By Noether's second theorem, local gauge invariance makes charge conservation an identity that Maxwell's equations themselves require.

registry.name: Phase matching as momentum conservation
registry.summary: Translation invariance of a homogeneous crystal conserves photon momentum in wave mixing, so efficient conversion needs Δk=0, usually reached through birefringence. Quasi-phase-matching deliberately reduces continuous to discrete translation symmetry with periodic poling. Momentum is then conserved only up to the grating's reciprocal vector.

registry.name: Plasma frequency as photon mass: Anderson's Higgs route
registry.summary: In a collisionless Drude medium, transverse light obeys ω²=ω_p²+c²k², a massive Klein–Gordon dispersion. The long-range Coulomb force lifts the would-be acoustic density mode to the plasmon at ω_p. Anderson used this plasma picture to argue that a gauge field can gain mass by absorbing a would-be Goldstone mode, the core of the Higgs–Anderson mechanism.
registry.breaks: A normal plasma has no condensate and no broken symmetry. A collisionless plasma only freezes in static magnetic flux, like a perfect conductor, while a superconductor expels it (Meissner effect) because its photon mass comes from a phase-coherent condensate. With collisions, static fields penetrate fully.

registry.name: Laser threshold as spontaneous U(1) phase breaking
registry.summary: Near threshold the single-mode field amplitude obeys a Landau-like equation. Below threshold only zero field is stable; above it there is a ring of states with fixed amplitude and arbitrary phase. The phase is then a Goldstone-like soft mode, and its diffusion under spontaneous-emission noise sets the Schawlow–Townes linewidth.
registry.breaks: A laser is an open, driven-dissipative system rather than an equilibrium ground state. A single mode is effectively zero-dimensional, so the phase diffuses freely (finite linewidth). There is no true long-range order or thermodynamic singularity, only a crossover that sharpens with photon number.
sources: Schawlow & Townes (1958). "Infrared and Optical Masers". *Phys. Rev.* 112, 1940. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940)

registry.name: Rayleigh's λ⁻⁴ law from dimensional analysis
registry.summary: Rayleigh (1871) argued that for a particle much smaller than the wavelength, the scattered amplitude is proportional to its volume and falls off as 1/r. Dimensional consistency then forces a 1/λ² factor in amplitude, hence λ⁻⁴ in intensity, which is why the sky is blue. It is the textbook example of a scaling argument.
registry.breaks: It holds only for size parameter 2πa/λ≪1 and away from resonances. For a≳λ the full Mie solution, with its resonances and nearly wavelength-independent scattering, takes over (white clouds).

registry.name: Mode-locked frequency combs as rulers for constants
registry.summary: A mode-locked laser emits a comb of evenly spaced frequencies, and f–2f self-referencing fixes its offset. This links optical frequencies to the caesium microwave standard, enabling hydrogen spectroscopy for the Rydberg constant and optical-clock limits on drifts of α. Earlier laser frequency and wavelength measurements had already led to fixing c exactly in 1983.

registry.summary: Until 2019 the ampere was defined by the magnetostatic force between parallel wires, which fixed μ0=4π×10⁻⁷ N A⁻² exactly. registry.summary: The second law is philosophy's central example of an irreversible macroscopic law resting on time-symmetric microdynamics. The standard reductive account combines $S=k_B\ln W$ with a low-entropy initial condition (the past hypothesis), and the status of that account is still debated.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Maxwell's demon and Landauer: is information physical?
registry.summary: In the Bennett–Landauer account, Maxwell's demon is defeated by the $k_BT\ln2$ cost of erasing its memory. Philosophers such as Earman and Norton dispute whether Landauer's principle is independently established, even though experiments have confirmed the erasure bound.
sources: Landauer (1961). "Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process". *IBM J. Res. Dev.* 5, 183. [doi:10.1147/rd.53.0183](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.53.0183)

registry.name: H-theorem and the Loschmidt–Zermelo objections
registry.summary: Boltzmann's H-theorem derives a monotonic entropy increase from the Boltzmann equation. Loschmidt's reversal objection and Zermelo's recurrence objection traced the time asymmetry to the molecular-chaos assumption (Stosszahlansatz), now the standard case study of irreversibility emerging from reversible laws.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Universality, emergence and the thermodynamic limit
registry.summary: Phase transitions are non-analyticities that exist only in the $N\to\infty$ limit, and universality makes critical exponents independent of microscopic detail. Both are the main case studies in the reduction-versus-emergence and multiple-realizability debates, from Anderson's 'More is different' to Batterman.
sources: Anderson (1972). "More Is Different". *Science* 177, 393. [doi:10.1126/science.177.4047.393](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.177.4047.393)

registry.name: Kramers–Kronig relations from causality
registry.summary: Causality makes the response function $\chi(\omega)$ analytic in the upper half-plane. Contour integration then gives the Kramers–Kronig relations between its reactive and dissipative parts, plus sum rules, and analytic continuation from Matsubara frequencies gives real-time response.
sources: Toll (1956). "Causality and the Dispersion Relation: Logical Foundations". *Phys. Rev.* 104, 1760. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.104.1760](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.104.1760)

registry.name: Lee–Yang zeros: transitions as complex zeros of Z
registry.summary: For finite N the partition function is a polynomial in the fugacity with no positive real zeros. The Lee–Yang circle theorem places every zero of the ferromagnetic Ising model on $|z|=1$, and a transition appears where the zeros pinch the real axis as $N\to\infty$; Fisher zeros do the same in complex β.
sources: Lee & Yang (1952). "Statistical Theory of Equations of State and Phase Transitions. II. Lattice Gas and Ising Model". *Phys. Rev.* 87, 410. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.87.410](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.87.410)

registry.name: Response functions are retarded Green's functions
registry.summary: The Kubo formula writes the susceptibility as a retarded commutator Green's function, so linear response is a Green's-function convolution with the force. Causality enters through $\theta(t)$, and the poles give the normal modes and their damping.
sources: Kubo (1957). "Statistical-Mechanical Theory of Irreversible Processes. I. General Theory and Simple Applications to Magnetic and Conduction Problems". *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 12, 570. [doi:10.1143/JPSJ.12.570](https://doi.org/10.1143/JPSJ.12.570)

registry.name: Fokker–Planck propagators as Green's functions
registry.summary: The transition probability of Brownian motion is the Green's function (heat kernel) of the diffusion or Fokker–Planck operator. First-passage and escape problems are solved with images, Laplace transforms and Sturm–Liouville eigenmodes, and the symmetrized Fokker–Planck operator maps onto a Schrödinger operator.
sources: Chandrasekhar (1943). "Stochastic Problems in Physics and Astronomy". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 15, 1. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.15.1](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.15.1)

Kramers (1940). "Brownian motion in a field of force and the diffusion model of chemical reactions". *Physica* 7, 284. [doi:10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90098-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0031-8914(40)90098-2)

registry.name: Transfer-matrix eigenvalues give the free energy
registry.summary: With local couplings, $Z=\mathrm{Tr}\,T^N$, so the free energy comes from the largest transfer-matrix eigenvalue and the correlation length from the ratio of the top two. Perron–Frobenius makes the top eigenvalue unique, which rules out a 1D transition at T>0, and Onsager solved 2D Ising by diagonalizing its transfer matrix.
sources: Kramers & Wannier (1941). "Statistics of the Two-Dimensional Ferromagnet. Part I". *Phys. Rev.* 60, 252. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.60.252](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.60.252)
Onsager (1944). "Crystal Statistics. I. A Two-Dimensional Model with an Order-Disorder Transition". *Phys. Rev.* 65, 117. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.65.117](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.65.117)

registry.name: Carathéodory: second law as integrability of δQ
registry.summary: In Carathéodory's formulation, heat is an inexact Pfaffian 1-form. The axiom that every state has adiabatically inaccessible neighbours implies the form is integrable, and its integrating factor yields absolute temperature and entropy from differential geometry alone.
sources: Lieb & Yngvason (1999). "The physics and mathematics of the second law of thermodynamics". *Phys. Rep.* 310, 1. [doi:10.1016/S0370-1573(98)00082-9](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0370-1573(98)00082-9)

registry.name: Canonical energy fluctuations limit microcalorimeters
registry.summary: A microcalorimeter or bolometer weakly linked to a bath has canonical energy fluctuations $\langle\Delta E^2\rangle=k_BT^2C$. This thermodynamic-fluctuation noise sets the ultimate resolution of transition-edge sensors, which is why they operate near 0.1 K with tiny heat capacity.
sources: Irwin (1995). "An application of electrothermal feedback for high resolution cryogenic particle detection". *Appl. Phys. Lett.* 66, 1998. [doi:10.1063/1.113674](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.113674)

registry.name: Johnson–Nyquist noise as fluctuation–dissipation
registry.summary: The thermal noise floor $4k_BTR\Delta f$ of every resistor and amplifier is the fluctuation–dissipation theorem applied to a circuit. The theorem's quantum form adds the zero-point term behind the half-photon-per-mode limit of linear amplifiers.
sources: Nyquist (1928). "Thermal Agitation of Electric Charge in Conductors". *Phys. Rev.* 32, 110. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.32.110](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.32.110)
Callen & Welton (1951). "Irreversibility and Generalized Noise". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 34. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.34](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.34)

registry.name: Phase transitions in high-dimensional inference
registry.summary: Planted (teacher–student) problems such as community detection, compressed sensing and perceptron learning are disordered systems, and replica or cavity calculations give their Bayes-optimal error. They show sharp detectability and algorithmic-hardness thresholds, and Bayes-optimal inference sits on the Nishimori line, where replica symmetry holds.
sources: Zdeborová & Krzakala (2016). "Statistical physics of inference: thresholds and algorithms". *Adv. Phys.* 65, 453. [doi:10.1080/00018732.2016.1211393](https://doi.org/10.1080/00018732.2016.1211393)
Gardner (1988). "The space of interactions in neural network models". *J. Phys. A* 21, 257. [doi:10.1088/0305-4470/21/1/030](https://doi.org/10.1088/0305-4470/21/1/030)

registry.name: Maximum entropy: statistical mechanics as inference
registry.summary: Jaynes showed that the Gibbs ensembles are the maximum-Shannon-entropy distributions consistent with measured averages, so inference and statistical mechanics share the exponential family. In Bayesian terms the evidence plays the role of a partition function and $-\ln$(evidence) that of a free energy.
registry.map: \max_p\Big[-\sum p\ln p\Big]\ \text{s.t.}\ \langle E\rangle\ \Rightarrow\ p\propto e^{-\beta E}

registry.name: Cramér–Rao bound and thermodynamic uncertainty
registry.summary: The thermodynamic uncertainty relation bounds the relative precision of any current by the entropy produced. It follows from the Cramér–Rao inequality applied to a perturbed path ensemble, so dissipation plays the role of the Fisher information that limits precision.
sources: Barato & Seifert (2015). "Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation for Biomolecular Processes". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 114, 158101. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.114.158101](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.114.158101)

registry.name: Variational Bayes is mean-field theory
registry.summary: Fitting a factorized approximate posterior by maximizing the evidence lower bound is the Gibbs–Bogoliubov–Feynman variational principle of naive mean-field theory. Belief propagation corresponds to the Bethe approximation, and the TAP equations add the Onsager reaction term.

registry.name: Permutation symmetry gives Bose and Fermi statistics
registry.summary: Identical particles carry a one-dimensional representation of the permutation group $S_N$: symmetric for bosons, antisymmetric for fermions. These give Bose–Einstein and Fermi–Dirac occupation numbers, and in 2D the braid group also allows anyons.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Symmetry classifies phases and transitions
registry.summary: Phases differ by which subgroup $H\subset G$ of the symmetry group the state keeps, and the order parameter transforms in a representation of $G$. Together with the dimension, $G$ and $H$ fix the allowed Landau free energy, the order-parameter manifold $G/H$ and its defects, and the universality class.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Onsager reciprocity from time-reversal invariance
registry.summary: Time-reversal symmetry of the microscopic dynamics implies the Onsager–Casimir relations among transport coefficients, such as the Kelvin relation between the Peltier and Seebeck coefficients. The relations carry sign factors for T-odd variables and require reversing magnetic fields.
sources: Onsager (1931). "Reciprocal Relations in Irreversible Processes. I.". *Phys. Rev.* 37, 405. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.37.405](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.37.405)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Virasoro symmetry solves 2D critical models
registry.summary: At 2D critical points, scale invariance grows into the infinite-dimensional Virasoro algebra. Its unitary minimal-model representations give exact exponents, e.g. Ising with $c=1/2$, $\eta=1/4$, $\nu=1$, which match Onsager's lattice solution.
sources: Belavin, Polyakov & Zamolodchikov (1984). "Infinite conformal symmetry in two-dimensional quantum field theory". *Nucl. Phys. B* 241, 333. [doi:10.1016/0550-3213(84)90052-X](https://doi.org/10.1016/0550-3213(84)90052-X)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Order-parameter symmetry labels universality classes
registry.summary: A universality class is fixed by the dimension and the order parameter's symmetry group: Z2 (Ising), O(2) (XY, He-4), O(3) (Heisenberg) or S_q (Potts). The representation content of a perturbation, such as cubic anisotropy, decides whether it is relevant.
sources: Pelissetto & Vicari (2002). "Critical phenomena and renormalization-group theory". *Phys. Rep.* 368, 549. [doi:10.1016/S0370-1573(02)00219-3](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0370-1573(02)00219-3)

registry.name: Conserved charges fix the Gibbs ensemble
registry.summary: Each Noether charge (energy, U(1) particle number, momentum) enters the equilibrium ensemble with its own Lagrange multiplier ($\beta$, $\beta\mu$, $\beta\mathbf v$). Integrable systems, which have extensively many conserved quantities, relax instead to a generalized Gibbs ensemble.
sources: Rigol et al. (2007). "Relaxation in a Completely Integrable Many-Body Quantum System: An Ab Initio Study of the Dynamics of the Highly Excited States of 1D Lattice Hard-Core Bosons". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 98, 050405. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.98.050405](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.98.050405)

registry.name: Replica symmetry breaking vs. ordinary SSB
registry.summary: Parisi's solution of the SK model breaks the permutation symmetry among $n\to0$ replicas. The Edwards–Anderson overlap then acts as an order parameter for frozen random order, as ergodicity splits into many pure states.
registry.breaks: No symmetry of the physical Hamiltonian breaks: replica symmetry exists only inside the $n\to0$ formalism, and the pure states are not related by any group action. Whether finite-dimensional spin glasses follow RSB or the droplet picture is still disputed.
sources: Sherrington & Kirkpatrick (1975). "Solvable Model of a Spin-Glass". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 35, 1792. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.1792](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.35.1792)
Parisi (1979). "Infinite Number of Order Parameters for Spin-Glasses". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 43, 1754. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.43.1754)

registry.name: BEC as broken U(1); Goldstone modes set low-T laws
registry.summary: Bose–Einstein condensation is off-diagonal long-range order, a broken global U(1) phase whose Goldstone mode is the Bogoliubov phonon. More generally, Goldstone dispersion sets low-T power laws: linear phonons give Debye $C\propto T^3$, and quadratic ferromagnetic magnons give Bloch $\Delta M\propto T^{3/2}$.
sources: Penrose & Onsager (1956). "Bose-Einstein Condensation and Liquid Helium". *Phys. Rev.* 104, 576. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.104.576](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.104.576)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Landau free energy is the symmetry-breaking potential
registry.summary: The Landau expansion and the Mexican-hat (Higgs) potential are the same symmetric quartic, and its minimum moves off the origin when the quadratic coefficient changes sign. Mean-field theory then gives $m\propto(T_c-T)^{1/2}$, and the Ginzburg criterion says when fluctuations invalidate it.
registry.breaks: Landau theory is a thermal free energy with a T-dependent coefficient, valid above the upper critical dimension. When the symmetry is gauged there is no local gauge-invariant order parameter (Elitzur's theorem) and the Goldstone modes are absorbed by the gauge field.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Mermin–Wagner and quasi-long-range order
registry.summary: In 2D, Goldstone fluctuations forbid continuous symmetry breaking at T>0 (Mermin–Wagner), but the XY model still has a transition. Vortices, classified by $\pi_1(U(1))=\mathbb Z$, unbind at $T_{\rm BKT}$ and separate power-law from exponential correlations.
sources: Mermin & Wagner (1966). "Absence of Ferromagnetism or Antiferromagnetism in One- or Two-Dimensional Isotropic Heisenberg Models". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 17, 1133. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.1133](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.17.1133)

Kosterlitz & Thouless (1973). "Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems". *J. Phys. C* 6, 1181. [doi:10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010](https://doi.org/10.1088/0022-3719/6/7/010)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Anomalous dimensions: where naive scaling fails
registry.summary: Dimensional analysis and generalized homogeneity (Widom scaling) predict power laws, but near criticality the microscopic cutoff never drops out, so exponents pick up anomalous dimensions; Barenblatt calls this incomplete similarity. The RG computes them as eigenvalues at a fixed point.
sources: Wilson (1971). "Renormalization Group and Critical Phenomena. I. Renormalization Group and the Kadanoff Scaling Picture". *Phys. Rev. B* 4, 3174. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.4.3174)
Widom (1965). "Equation of State in the Neighborhood of the Critical Point". *J. Chem. Phys.* 43, 3898. [doi:10.1063/1.1696618](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1696618)
