registry.name: Skyrmions: baryons as topological solitons
registry.summary: In the Skyrme model, which the large-N_c limit of QCD motivates, the chiral pion Lagrangian supports stable topological solitons whose winding number is baryon number. Nucleons, nuclei and nuclear matter appear as classical field configurations quantized through their collective rotations, carrying the soliton idea from classical nonlinear waves into the strong force.
registry.breaks: Skyrmions are topological solitons, not integrable ones: there is no inverse scattering and they deform when they interact. The model overbinds light nuclei and has been superseded quantitatively by chiral EFT.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Surface vibrations: Rayleigh drop modes quantized
registry.summary: Quadrupole and octupole phonons in vibrational nuclei are the quantized normal modes of a charged liquid drop's surface, R(θ,φ) = R_0[1 + Σ α_λμ Y_λμ]. The restoring constant combines surface tension and Coulomb terms as in Rayleigh's capillary-oscillation analysis, which predicts two-phonon 0+, 2+, 4+ triplets near 2ħω.
registry.breaks: Measured mass parameters exceed irrotational-flow values, many supposedly vibrational nuclei miss the harmonic two-phonon pattern, and shell structure rather than surface tension sets most low-lying collectivity.
sources: Weizsäcker (1935). "Zur Theorie der Kernmassen". *Z. Phys.* 96, 431. [doi:10.1007/BF01337700](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01337700)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Superdeformation from 2:1 oscillator resonance
registry.summary: In the deformed (Nilsson) oscillator, whenever ω_⊥:ω_z is a ratio of small integers the classical orbits close into Lissajous figures and the quantum levels bunch into degenerate shells. The 2:1 resonance produces the superdeformed magic numbers and 3:1 gives hyperdeformation, the same commensurability that makes classical oscillator orbits periodic.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Giant resonances as acoustic modes of nucleon fluids
registry.summary: In the giant dipole resonance protons oscillate against neutrons. Goldhaber–Teller model it as two rigid spheres sloshing (E ∝ A^{-1/6}), Steinwedel–Jensen as a standing sound wave of isovector density in a fixed sphere (E ∝ A^{-1/3}), and the data interpolate between them; the isoscalar monopole breathing mode measures nuclear incompressibility.
registry.map: E_{\rm SJ}\propto A^{-1/3},\ E_{\rm GT}\propto A^{-1/6};\ E_{\rm GMR}=\hbar\sqrt{K_A/(m\langle r^2\rangle)}
registry.breaks: Nuclear sound is zero sound of a Fermi liquid (Fermi-surface distortion at ωτ ≫ 1), not collisional first sound, and the resonances are Landau-damped into particle–hole states.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Wobbling: quantized precession of a triaxial top
registry.summary: A triaxial nucleus with three distinct moments of inertia is a quantum asymmetric top. Bohr–Mottelson wobbling is the quantized small-amplitude precession of the rotation axis about the axis of largest inertia, the stable branch of Euler's tennis-racket analysis, and wobbling bands have been seen in odd-A Lu isotopes.
registry.map: \omega_{\rm wob}=\omega_{\rm rot}\sqrt{\frac{(\mathcal I_1-\mathcal I_2)(\mathcal I_1-\mathcal I_3)}{\mathcal I_2\mathcal I_3}}\ \leftrightarrow\ \text{Euler small-oscillation frequency}
registry.breaks: The moment hierarchy is set by quantum (irrotational-like) flow. An aligned high-j quasiparticle (transverse wobbling) changes the classical stability criterion, and some wobbling assignments are disputed.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Neutron-star moment of inertia and glitches
registry.summary: Pulsar spin-down, glitches and binary spin–orbit precession are rotational dynamics of a two-component body. A glitch transfers angular momentum from a superfluid component to the crust, so the crust's share of the moment of inertia constrains the EOS, and EOS-insensitive I–Love–Q relations tie the moment of inertia to tidal deformability and quadrupole.
sources: Lattimer & Prakash (2001). "Neutron star structure and the equation of state". *Astrophys. J.* 550, 426. [arXiv:astro-ph/0002232](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0002232)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Rotational bands: the quantized rotor and its inertia
registry.summary: Deformed nuclei show bands E_J = ħ²J(J+1)/2𝓘, the spectrum of a quantized free rotor with E(4+)/E(2+) = 10/3. The moment of inertia is the classical quantity, and its measured value, which lies between the irrotational-flow and rigid-body values, directly probes nuclear superfluidity.
registry.map: E_J=\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mathcal I}J(J+1)\leftrightarrow T=\frac{L^2}{2I},\quad \mathcal I_{\rm irr}<\mathcal I_{\rm exp}<\mathcal I_{\rm rig}
registry.breaks: There is no collective rotation about a symmetry axis (quantum indistinguishability). 𝓘 is far from rigid: pairing reduces it to roughly 30–50% of the rigid value, and it changes with spin (Coriolis anti-pairing, backbending).

registry.name: Onsager quantization of cyclotron orbits
registry.summary: Quantum oscillations follow from Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization of semiclassical cyclotron orbits on the Fermi surface: the action variable of the orbit fixes allowed k-space areas, so dHvA and SdH frequencies measure extremal Fermi-surface cross sections.

registry.name: Berry curvature deforms semiclassical phase space
registry.summary: Semiclassical Bloch electrons with Berry curvature obey non-canonical Hamiltonian dynamics: the anomalous velocity appears and Liouville's phase-space volume is not conserved unless weighted by (1+e B.Omega/hbar), which corrects the density of states.

registry.name: Continuum mechanics of soft materials
registry.summary: Soft matter is described at long wavelengths by continuum theories (viscoelastic fluids, gels, nematic hydrodynamics, granular rheology) built on the conservation laws and constitutive-relation framework of continuum mechanics.

registry.name: Dislocations as topological defects of elastic crystals
registry.summary: Plastic deformation of crystals proceeds by motion of dislocations, line defects labelled by a Burgers vector, whose long-range stress fields are solutions of continuum elasticity; their unbinding drives KTHNY two-dimensional melting.

registry.name: Elastic waves as long-wavelength acoustic phonons
registry.summary: Acoustic phonon branches at small k are the elastic waves of continuum elasticity: their slopes are the longitudinal and transverse sound speeds fixed by elastic constants, which phonon dispersion measurements determine.

registry.name: Contact mechanics, force chains and the Janssen effect
registry.summary: Static granular packs transmit stress through heterogeneous force chains between Hertzian contacts; frictional wall support saturates pressure with depth in silos (Janssen effect), so granular stress cannot be treated as hydrostatic.

registry.name: Maxwell counting and isostatic jamming
registry.summary: Maxwell's 1864 constraint counting for the rigidity of frames gives the isostatic contact number z=2d at the jamming transition; above jamming, shear modulus and excess contacts grow as power laws of compression.

registry.name: Frank orientational elasticity and liquid-crystal elastomers
registry.summary: Frank theory is an elasticity for the director field (splay, twist, bend) instead of displacements; coupling it to a rubber network gives liquid-crystal elastomers with 'soft elasticity' and large reversible actuation.
registry.breaks: The director is a unit headless vector, so Frank elasticity has topological defects and no restoring force for uniform rotations; a fluid nematic has zero shear modulus, unlike a solid.

registry.name: Rubber elasticity: entropic springs to neo-Hookean solids
registry.summary: Each network strand is an entropic Gaussian spring, so averaging over strands gives the neo-Hookean strain-energy function of finite-strain continuum elasticity with shear modulus n k_B T, explaining why rubber stiffens on heating.
sources: Treloar & Montgomery (1949). "The physics of rubber elasticity". *Phys. Today*. [doi:10.1063/1.3060678](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.3060678)

registry.name: Topological mechanics of isostatic lattices
registry.summary: Band topology applied to the compatibility matrix of Maxwell (isostatic) lattices predicts floppy zero modes localized on particular edges, an index theorem for mechanical metamaterials analogous to the SSH chain.

registry.name: Electron hydrodynamics in graphene
registry.summary: When electron-electron collisions dominate over impurity and phonon scattering, electrons in clean graphene flow as a viscous fluid obeying Navier-Stokes-like equations, producing negative nonlocal resistance from backflow whirlpools and Poiseuille profiles.
sources: Bandurin et al. (2016). "Negative local resistance caused by viscous electron backflow in graphene". *Science* 351, 1055. [doi:10.1126/science.aad0201](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aad0201)

registry.name: mu(I) rheology: granular matter as a viscoplastic fluid
registry.summary: Dense granular flows obey a local friction law in which the effective friction depends on the inertial number; inserted into continuum momentum equations it predicts flows on inclines, in silos and in rotating drums.
sources: Jop, Forterre & Pouliquen (2006). "A constitutive law for dense granular flows". *Nature* 441, 727. [doi:10.1038/nature04801](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature04801)

registry.name: Nematodynamics: anisotropic viscous flow
registry.summary: Ericksen-Leslie theory couples the Navier-Stokes equations to director rotation, giving three Miesowicz viscosities, flow alignment and backflow; it controls display switching times and active-nematic hydrodynamics.
sources: Leslie (1968). "Some constitutive equations for liquid crystals". *Arch. Ration. Mech. Anal.* 28, 265. [doi:10.1007/BF00251810](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00251810)

registry.name: Electroconvection in nematics
registry.summary: Above a threshold voltage nematic layers develop convection rolls (Williams domains) through the Carr-Helfrich mechanism, an anisotropic analogue of Rayleigh-Benard convection and a classic system for pattern formation and spatiotemporal chaos.
sources: Cross & Hohenberg (1993). "Pattern formation outside of equilibrium". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 65, 851. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851)

registry.name: Colloids, polymers and swimmers in Stokes flow
registry.summary: Soft-matter dynamics is overdamped: colloid diffusion, polymer Rouse-Zimm dynamics and microswimming are governed by Stokes drag and long-range hydrodynamic interactions (Oseen tensor).

registry.name: Microswimmers at low Reynolds number
registry.summary: Bacteria and synthetic swimmers live at Re~1e-5, where Purcell's scallop theorem forbids reciprocal strokes and Stokesian far fields (pusher/puller force dipoles) set their collective hydrodynamics and active stresses.

registry.name: Stokes drag and diffusion of colloids
registry.summary: Colloid diffusion follows from Stokes drag via the Einstein relation, and sedimentation, hydrodynamic interactions and lubrication forces between colloids are low-Reynolds-number flow problems.

registry.name: Active turbulence versus inertial turbulence
registry.summary: Dense bacterial suspensions and active nematics show chaotic mesoscale vortices with power-law energy spectra at Reynolds numbers far below 1, driven by active stress rather than inertia.
registry.map: E(k)\sim k^{-5/3}\ (\text{Kolmogorov, inertial})\ \text{vs}\ E(k)\ \text{power laws set by active length }\ell_a=\sqrt{K/|\zeta|}
registry.breaks: Energy is injected at every scale by active stress and dissipated by viscosity, with no inertial cascade; the vortex size is set by an active length, and spectral exponents are not universal.
sources: Wensink et al. (2012). "Meso-scale turbulence in living fluids". *Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci.* 109, 14308. [doi:10.1073/pnas.1202032109](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1202032109)

registry.name: Polymer drag reduction and elastic turbulence
registry.summary: Dilute long polymers reduce turbulent drag by up to ~80% (Toms effect) by suppressing near-wall vortices, and in viscous flows polymer elasticity alone drives chaotic 'elastic turbulence' at Reynolds numbers far below 1.
sources: Groisman & Steinberg (2000). "Elastic turbulence in a polymer solution flow". *Nature* 405, 53. [doi:10.1038/35011019](https://doi.org/10.1038/35011019)

registry.name: Inelastic collisions and granular gases
registry.summary: Grains collide with a restitution coefficient below 1, so a granular gas loses energy in every collision; the resulting homogeneous cooling (Haff's law) and clustering instability follow from momentum conservation with kinetic-energy loss.
sources: Haff (1983). "Grain flow as a fluid-mechanical phenomenon". *J. Fluid Mech.* 134, 401. [doi:10.1017/S0022112083003419](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022112083003419)

registry.name: Chaotic billiards and mesoscopic conductance fluctuations
registry.summary: Ballistic quantum dots whose classical shape gives chaotic trajectories show universal conductance fluctuations and weak-localization lineshapes governed by random-matrix theory, while regular (integrable) shapes do not; classical chaos thus controls quantum transport statistics.
sources: Marcus et al. (1992). "Conductance fluctuations and chaotic scattering in ballistic microstructures". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 69, 506. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.506](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.506)

registry.name: Frenkel-Kontorova model and the standard map
registry.summary: Ground states of the Frenkel-Kontorova model of an incommensurate adsorbate or modulated crystal correspond to orbits of an area-preserving twist map; Aubry's pinning transition, where the incommensurate phase locks to the lattice, is the breakup of a KAM torus, and the devil's staircase of commensurate phases follows.

registry.name: FPUT anharmonic lattice and the discovery of solitons
registry.summary: The 1955 Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou simulation of an anharmonic atomic chain failed to thermalize its phonon modes; Zabusky and Kruskal's continuum limit, the KdV equation, explained the recurrence and introduced the soliton.

registry.name: Magnetic skyrmions as topological solitons
registry.summary: Skyrmions are localized, particle-like solutions of the nonlinear micromagnetic field equations, stable because of an integer winding number, the topological-soliton class first introduced by Skyrme for nucleons.

registry.name: Fluxons in long Josephson junctions are sine-Gordon solitons
registry.summary: The phase difference along a long Josephson junction obeys the sine-Gordon equation; its kink solitons are fluxons carrying one flux quantum, which move relativistically at the Swihart velocity and underlie flux-flow oscillators.

registry.name: SSH domain-wall solitons and topological zero modes
registry.summary: Domain walls between the two dimerization patterns of polyacetylene are solitons that bind a mid-gap zero mode with fractional charge or reversed spin-charge relation; the SSH chain is now the prototype 1D topological insulator (Jackiw-Rebbi index).
sources: Su, Schrieffer & Heeger (1979). "Solitons in Polyacetylene". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 42, 1698. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.42.1698](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.42.1698)

registry.name: Flocking as synchronization in space
registry.summary: Alignment of headings in the Vicsek model is Kuramoto-like phase synchronization of self-propelled oscillators, with the twist that particles move and so couplings change; both show noise-driven order-disorder transitions.
registry.breaks: Vicsek particles move, so the coupling network changes with the order itself, giving density bands and giant number fluctuations that have no counterpart in fixed-network Kuramoto models; their order parameter is a vector, not a phase.

registry.name: Synchronization of Josephson-junction arrays
registry.summary: Series arrays of current-biased junctions coupled through a shared load map onto the Kuramoto model and phase-lock, the route to coherent microwave emission; Shapiro steps are Arnold-tongue frequency locking of a junction to an external drive.
sources: Wiesenfeld, Colet & Strogatz (1996). "Synchronization Transitions in a Disordered Josephson Series Array". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 76, 404. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.76.404](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.76.404)

registry.name: Phonons as quantized normal modes
registry.summary: Phonons are the quantized normal modes of the crystal's coupled harmonic oscillators; each mode contributes hbar*omega(n+1/2), giving Debye and Einstein heat capacities.

registry.name: Normal-mode analysis behind lattice dynamics

registry.name: Monatomic and diatomic chains to phonon branches

registry.name: Drude and Lorentz models as damped driven oscillators

registry.name: Einstein-de Haas and Barnett effects
registry.summary: Reversing a ferromagnet's magnetization makes the free body rotate (Einstein-de Haas), and rotating a body magnetizes it (Barnett), because total spin plus rigid-body angular momentum is conserved; these measured the electron g-factor and now enable ultrafast demagnetization studies.

registry.name: Normal modes of the Sun

registry.name: Baryon acoustic oscillations as sound waves

registry.name: Parametric resonance in preheating

registry.name: Spin-orbit dynamics and chaotic tumbling

registry.name: Rigid rotation, free precession and pulsars

registry.name: Axial precession and obliquity climate cycles

registry.name: Adiabatic invariants as action variables

registry.name: Vlasov equation as Liouville flow

registry.name: Guiding-centre Hamiltonian dynamics

registry.name: Radiation belts and three adiabatic invariants

registry.name: Gyrokinetics from Lagrangian field theory

registry.name: Variational MHD equilibrium and stability

registry.name: MHD as continuum mechanics

registry.name: MHD as fluid mechanics plus Lorentz force

registry.name: Parker wind as transonic nozzle flow

registry.name: Laser-plasma hydrodynamic instabilities

registry.name: Rayleigh–Taylor in ICF implosions

registry.name: Convection-driven dynamos

registry.name: MHD instabilities as magnetised RT/KH

registry.name: Kinetic vs fluid instability analyses

registry.name: Ion-acoustic and Kelvin–Helmholtz in plasmas

registry.name: Plasma turbulence and fluid turbulence

registry.name: Turbulent dynamo and mean-field theory
registry.summary: Turbulent flows stretch, twist and fold field lines, giving small-scale dynamos and mean-field α-effect; the shared accretion-disk paper links turbulence, MRI and transport.

registry.name: Kolmogorov cascade to MHD cascade

registry.name: MHD turbulence extends Kolmogorov theory

registry.name: Shock jump conditions as conservation laws
registry.summary: Rankine–Hugoniot conditions are mass, momentum and energy conservation across a discontinuity; collisionless shocks satisfy them via field-mediated dissipation instead of collisions.

registry.name: Lorentz force and Coriolis force

registry.name: Field-line flow as Hamiltonian system, KAM surfaces

registry.name: Particle trapping and quasilinear resonance overlap
registry.summary: Nonlinear Landau damping and particle trapping in a wave potential produce pendulum-like islands in phase space; overlapping waves yield Chirikov chaos underlying quasilinear diffusion.

registry.name: Adiabatic invariant breakdown and chaos

registry.name: Nonlinear wake waves and wave breaking
registry.summary: Plasma wakes are nonlinear Langmuir waves whose steepening and wave-breaking limit sets accelerating gradients, comparable to nonlinear wave steepening and soliton formation in dispersive media.

registry.name: Ion-acoustic solitons and KdV
registry.summary: Weakly nonlinear ion-acoustic waves reduce to the KdV equation via reductive perturbation, giving solitons; Washimi–Taniuti derivation was a landmark. Alfvén waves yield DNLS.

registry.name: Plasmoid chain formation as pattern formation
registry.summary: Plasmoid instability of reconnection current sheets spontaneously produces hierarchical island chains from a tearing instability, analogous to pattern-forming instabilities.

registry.name: Landau damping and Kuramoto synchronization
registry.summary: Kuramoto oscillators with a frequency distribution obey a Vlasov-like continuum equation; incoherent-state stability and decay of the order parameter mirror Landau damping, as does the Case–Van Kampen analysis.

registry.name: Dust crystal lattice phonons
registry.summary: Dusty-plasma crystals support lattice phonons observable by video microscopy; they are screened-Coulomb (Yukawa) chains and lattices with normal modes, allowing atomic-scale dynamics at the particle level.

registry.name: Plasma oscillation as collective normal mode
registry.summary: Langmuir oscillation at ω_p is a collective harmonic mode of displaced electron sheets, and plasma waves are dispersive normal modes of a continuum of coupled oscillators.

registry.name: Magnetosonic and acoustic waves

registry.name: Ponderomotive force and Kapitza pendulum

registry.name: Parametric instabilities and Mathieu resonance

registry.name: Action–angle variables and Courant–Snyder invariant

registry.name: Ocean circulation as rotating viscous flow

registry.name: Atmospheric turbulence and cascades

registry.name: Rutherford scattering and molecular beam collisions

registry.name: Resonances and N-body methods in accelerators
registry.summary: Resonance overlap, secular perturbation theory and symplectic integrators from celestial mechanics are used for accelerator tracking and long-term stability. Space-charge tracking is an N-body problem.

registry.name: Rotating-frame physics of the planet

registry.name: Coriolis force and geostrophic balance
registry.summary: The Coriolis force from Earth's rotation balances pressure gradients to give geostrophic wind and drives cyclone rotation and Rossby waves.

registry.name: Rossby waves from the beta effect

registry.name: Tipping points as bifurcations

registry.name: AMOC bistability (Stommel model)

registry.name: Lorenz chaos and weather predictability
registry.summary: Lorenz's truncated convection model gave the first strange attractor. The result sets the finite predictability horizon of weather (~2 weeks), set by Lyapunov growth of errors.

registry.name: KAM tori and dynamic aperture
registry.summary: Nonlinear magnet errors make betatron motion a perturbed Hamiltonian system. Resonance islands, chaotic layers and surviving KAM tori set the dynamic aperture and beam lifetime.

registry.name: Solitons, tsunamis and internal waves

registry.name: Reaction–diffusion patterning of cell polarity

registry.name: Turing patterns and Kuramoto sync in biology
registry.summary: Developmental patterning follows Turing reaction–diffusion instabilities, and neural and circadian rhythms follow Kuramoto-type phase locking.

registry.name: Molecular vibrations as normal modes
registry.summary: Molecular vibrational spectra are the normal modes of coupled atoms on a potential surface, found by diagonalising the mass-weighted Hessian, as for coupled springs.

registry.name: Earth's free oscillations as normal modes
registry.summary: After large earthquakes the Earth rings in toroidal and spheroidal normal modes. These are the eigenmodes of a continuum coupled-oscillator system and constrain the PREM structure.

registry.name: Cavity resonance and Q factor in RF cavities
registry.summary: Accelerator RF cavities are driven resonators characterised by Q and bandwidth, and superconducting cavities reach Q of 10^10 or more. Their response follows the driven damped oscillator.

registry.name: Larmor precession and resonance in MRI
registry.summary: Nuclear spin in MRI follows classical gyroscopic precession and driven resonance, with Bloch-equation relaxation like a damped driven oscillator (T1, T2).

registry.name: Ocean waves, tides and dispersion
registry.summary: Surface gravity waves, internal waves and tides obey dispersion relations for fluid waves. The deep-water relation gives dispersive group and phase speeds.

registry.name: Wave propagation in the Earth
registry.summary: Seismology applies reflection, refraction, impedance and dispersion of mechanical waves to layered media. Surface waves, free oscillations and travel-time inversion probe structure.

registry.name: Acoustics underlying ultrasound imaging
registry.summary: Echography relies on impedance mismatch reflection, attenuation, Doppler shift and beamforming of acoustic waves in tissue. Elastography uses shear wave speed to measure stiffness.

registry.name: Medical acoustics: impedance and Doppler
registry.summary: Ultrasound transducers, tissue attenuation and Doppler blood-flow measurement are applications of acoustic wave theory.

registry.name: Mathieu/Hill equation and strong focusing
registry.summary: Betatron motion in an alternating-gradient lattice obeys Hill's equation, a periodically driven oscillator like Mathieu's. Stability bands match parametric resonance, and alternating focusing resembles Kapitza stabilisation.

registry.name: Gyroscope sensing, classical to atomic
registry.summary: Mechanical gyroscopes sense rotation via angular momentum conservation, and atom-interferometric gyroscopes measure the same Sagnac-type rotation with matter waves at far higher sensitivity.

registry.name: Earth's precession, nutation and inner core
registry.summary: Precession and nutation of Earth's axis depend on its moment of inertia and on core structure, so the free core nutation constrains interior properties.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Moment of inertia constrains density profile
registry.summary: Earth's moment of inertia factor (about 0.33) is a global constraint on radial density models such as PREM, showing a centrally condensed structure.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Laser linewidth sets temporal coherence
registry.summary: By the Wiener–Khinchin theorem the coherence time is the inverse spectral width, so the Schawlow–Townes linewidth fixes a laser's coherence length. Above threshold the intensity statistics change from thermal (g2(0)=2) to Poissonian (g2(0)=1), which separates a laser from a filtered thermal source of the same bandwidth.
sources: Schawlow & Townes (1958). "Infrared and Optical Masers". *Phys. Rev.* 112, 1940. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Dynamic light scattering via intensity correlations
registry.summary: Light scattered by many diffusing particles forms a fluctuating Gaussian speckle field. The Siegert relation then gives the field correlation from the measured intensity correlation, and its decay rate Dq² yields particle size via Stokes–Einstein. This is the Hanbury Brown–Twiss intensity-correlation method of statistical optics applied to scattering.
registry.breaks: The Siegert relation holds only for Gaussian (many-scatterer) fields. Few scatterers, non-ergodic samples or multiple scattering (which needs diffusing-wave spectroscopy) break it.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Superlenses beat the diffraction limit via evanescent waves
registry.summary: Fourier optics locates the diffraction limit: spatial frequencies above nk0 are evanescent and never reach the far field. Pendry's n=−1 slab amplifies these components and restores them in the image. Silver superlenses and hyperbolic hyperlenses achieve partial versions.
registry.breaks: Absorption and any deviation from ε=−1 limit the amplification, so resolution degrades with loss. The effect works only in the near field, within a fraction of a wavelength.
sources: Pendry (2000). "Negative Refraction Makes a Perfect Lens". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 85, 3966. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Space–time duality: diffraction ↔ dispersion
registry.summary: The paraxial diffraction equation for a beam and the pulse equation with group-velocity dispersion are the same Schrödinger-type equation, with transverse position swapped for retarded time. A quadratic temporal phase therefore acts as a 'time lens'. Stretchers, compressors (as used in chirped-pulse amplification), temporal imaging and the time–bandwidth product are the temporal counterparts of Fresnel propagation, lenses and the space–bandwidth limit.
registry.breaks: Time is one-dimensional and causal. Diffraction matches only anomalous dispersion, while dispersion can take either sign and has higher orders (β3) with no diffraction counterpart. Time lenses need electro-optic or nonlinear phase modulation, not glass.
sources: Strickland & Mourou (1985). "Compression of amplified chirped optical pulses". *Opt. Commun.* 56, 219. [doi:10.1016/0030-4018(85)90120-8](https://doi.org/10.1016/0030-4018(85)90120-8)

registry.name: Diffraction imaging: scattering amplitude as Fourier transform
registry.summary: In the first Born approximation the far-field scattering amplitude is the Fourier transform of the scatterer's density at q=k_out−k_in. X-ray and coherent diffraction imaging are thus Fourier optics with the phase lost, recovered by oversampled phase retrieval or by a holographic reference wave (Gabor).
registry.map: f(\mathbf q)\propto\int\rho(\mathbf r)e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r}d^3r,\qquad |\mathbf q|=2k\sin(\theta/2)
registry.breaks: Valid only for weak single scattering. Multiple scattering and absorption (dynamical diffraction) break the plain Fourier relation, and detectors record only |f|².
sources: Gabor (1948). "A New Microscopic Principle". *Nature* 161, 777. [doi:10.1038/161777a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/161777a0)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Ray optics as the eikonal limit of Maxwell waves
registry.summary: Writing the field as a slowly varying amplitude times e^{ik_0S} and keeping leading order in λ/L reduces the wave equation to the eikonal equation. Its characteristics are rays obeying Fermat's principle, the next order gives intensity transport along ray tubes, and Snell's law is the interface limit of the plane-wave boundary conditions.
registry.breaks: Fails near caustics, foci, shadow edges and features ≲λ, where diffraction (Kirchhoff, Keller's GTD) is needed. Polarization appears only at the next order (Rytov rotation).
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Resonator stability and Gaussian beams via ABCD matrices
registry.summary: Paraxial ray-transfer matrices decide whether a laser cavity is stable: rays stay bounded over many round trips if and only if |A+D|/2≤1, i.e. 0≤g1g2≤1. Kogelnik's ABCD law propagates the Gaussian beam's complex q parameter with the same matrices, which gives the cavity's mode size and waist.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Generalized Snell's law and negative refraction
registry.summary: Snell's law follows from continuity of the tangential phase. With n<0 the refracted ray bends to the same side of the normal (Veselago). A metasurface's abrupt phase gradient dΦ/dx adds tangential momentum, giving the generalized laws of reflection and refraction behind flat lenses. Graded-index designs (Luneburg lens, Maxwell fish-eye) are the ray limit of transformation optics.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Thin films are transmission-line impedance transformers
registry.summary: At normal incidence, waves in layered dielectrics obey the same transfer-matrix (telegrapher) equations as a transmission line with impedance Z0/n. A quarter-wave antireflection coating is therefore a quarter-wave matching transformer, and a Bragg mirror is a periodic line with a stop band.
registry.breaks: At oblique incidence the effective impedance depends on polarization (s: Z∝1/(n cosθ), p: Z∝cosθ/n), so a coating designed for one angle and polarization is mismatched for others.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Laser cavity as Fabry–Pérot; Fox–Li diffraction modes
registry.summary: A laser resonator is a Fabry–Pérot interferometer with gain: its longitudinal modes are the transmission peaks spaced by the free spectral range, and its passive linewidth is FSR divided by finesse. Fox and Li obtained the transverse modes as self-reproducing patterns of repeated Fresnel diffraction between the mirrors, with diffraction loss set by the Fresnel number.
sources: Schawlow & Townes (1958). "Infrared and Optical Masers". *Phys. Rev.* 112, 1940. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.112.1940)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Smith–Purcell radiation: a grating equation for moving charges
registry.summary: A charge skimming a periodic grating radiates because the grating's reciprocal vectors couple its evanescent, slower-than-light field to free-space waves. The emitted wavelength obeys the grating equation with the source's phase velocity set by the electron speed. This is Cherenkov phase matching with grating momentum in place of the medium's index.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Antenna arrays and apertures are Fraunhofer diffraction
registry.summary: A phased array's far field is the element pattern times an array factor that is the N-slit grating function. A progressive phase steers the main lobe, just as oblique incidence shifts a grating's orders. An aperture antenna's pattern is the Fraunhofer transform of its aperture field, so its beamwidth is the same λ/D as a diffraction-limited lens.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Faraday rotation and c=1/√(ε0μ0): light joins EM
registry.summary: Faraday's 1845 discovery that a magnetic field rotates the plane of polarization was the first evidence that light is electromagnetic. Maxwell's displacement current then predicted transverse waves at 1/√(ε0μ0), matching the measured speed of light, so polarization became the direction of the transverse E field.
sources: Maxwell (1865). "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 155, 459. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1865.0008](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1865.0008)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Crystal optics from the dielectric tensor
registry.summary: Birefringence is the anisotropic linear response of fields in matter. A symmetric tensor ε_ij makes D non-parallel to E, so the Poynting vector walks off from k, and each propagation direction has two orthogonally polarized eigenmodes, organized by the index ellipsoid. Crystal symmetry fixes whether the medium is isotropic, uniaxial or biaxial.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Birefringent phase matching and electro-optic χ(2)
registry.summary: Crystal birefringence makes efficient harmonic generation possible: picking the propagation angle so that n_e(2ω,θ)=n_o(ω) gives Δk=0 (type-I phase matching). The Pockels and Kerr electro-optic effects of crystal optics are χ(2)(ω;ω,0) and χ(3)(ω;ω,0,0) with a DC field; the lithium-niobate r_33 coefficient drives Mach–Zehnder modulators.
sources: Franken et al. (1961). "Generation of Optical Harmonics". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 7, 118. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.7.118)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Gyrotropy: magneto-optic non-reciprocity enables one-way modes
registry.summary: Faraday rotation comes from an imaginary antisymmetric off-diagonal permittivity or permeability (gyrotropy) induced by a magnetic field. This breaks reciprocity, which is why optical isolators work. Gyromagnetic photonic crystals use the same broken time-reversal symmetry to open bands with nonzero Chern number, giving the first one-way photonic edge states (Haldane–Raghu proposal, microwave YIG experiment).
sources: Ozawa et al. (2019). "Topological photonics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 015006. [arXiv:1802.04173](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04173)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Radiation reaction: the Abraham–Lorentz–Dirac force
registry.summary: The energy and momentum carried off by Larmor radiation imply a self-force on the charge. Dirac's covariant derivation from the retarded-minus-advanced self-field gives the Abraham–Lorentz–Dirac equation, which reduces to the Abraham–Lorentz force at low speed.
registry.breaks: The ALD equation has runaway and pre-acceleration solutions. In practice the reduced-order Landau–Lifshitz form is used, valid when the force changes slowly over r_e/c.
sources: Dirac (1938). "Classical theory of radiating electrons". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 167, 148. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1938.0124](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1938.0124)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Lorentz–Drude ε(ω), Kramers–Kronig and skin depth
registry.summary: The frequency-dependent response from fields in matter, with bound electrons as damped Lorentz oscillators and free electrons as the ω0=0 Drude case, determines how waves propagate. It sets dispersion, absorption lines, the plasma frequency below which metals reflect, and the skin depth. Causality links Re ε and Im ε through Kramers–Kronig.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Optical fibres and chips as dielectric waveguides
registry.summary: Fibre and on-chip guides are solved with the same Maxwell boundary-value problem as microwave waveguides: guided modes, cutoffs, group-velocity dispersion and coupled-mode theory. Confinement comes from total internal reflection at an index step instead of metal walls, and a step-index fibre is single-mode for V<2.405.
registry.breaks: Unlike a hollow metal guide, the fundamental mode of a dielectric guide has no cutoff, and its field reaches evanescently into the cladding, which allows bend loss and evanescent coupling.
sources: Kao & Hockham (1966). "Dielectric-fibre surface waveguides for optical frequencies". *Proc. IEE* 113, 1151. [doi:10.1049/piee.1966.0189](https://doi.org/10.1049/piee.1966.0189)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Surface plasmon polaritons as bound TM interface waves
registry.summary: Maxwell's equations with Fresnel boundary conditions at a metal–dielectric interface admit a bound TM surface wave whenever ε_m<−ε_d; it is the pole of the p-polarized reflection coefficient. Combined with the Drude permittivity and conductor skin depth, this gives the SPP dispersion, sub-wavelength confinement and propagation loss.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Refractive index as coherent forward scattering
registry.summary: By the Ewald–Oseen extinction theorem, radiation from the induced dipoles cancels the incident wave inside a medium and replaces it with a wave of phase velocity c/n. The index follows from the forward scattering amplitude, and the optical theorem ties its imaginary part to extinction, i.e. attenuation.
registry.breaks: The simple formula holds for dilute media (|n−1|≪1). Dense media need local-field (Lorentz–Lorenz) corrections.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Transformation optics: form-invariance of Maxwell's equations
registry.summary: Maxwell's equations keep their form under any coordinate map if ε and μ are replaced by transformed tensors. A desired light path, such as one bending around a hole, thus becomes a material prescription. Cloaks, concentrators and illusion devices are designed this way and built from metamaterials.
registry.breaks: Ideal cloaks need singular, anisotropic and dispersive parameters, so causality restricts them to narrow bands and approximate versions. Eikonal-only (ray) cloaks relax these requirements.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Maxwell's master equation as a topological band problem
registry.summary: In a lossless periodic medium Maxwell's equations become a Hermitian eigenproblem for H. Photonic Bloch modes therefore carry Berry connections and Chern numbers just as electron bands do, which lets band topology, bulk–edge correspondence and one-way edge waveguides carry over to optics.
registry.breaks: Photons are bosons with no Fermi level, so there is no quantized transport response. Gain, loss and material dispersion make the problem non-Hermitian or require auxiliary fields.
sources: Ozawa et al. (2019). "Topological photonics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 015006. [arXiv:1802.04173](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04173)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Synthetic gauge fields: Peierls phases for neutral photons
registry.summary: Photons carry no charge, but engineered direction-dependent hopping phases in coupled-resonator or waveguide lattices play the role of (q/ħ)∫A·dl. They create an effective magnetic flux per plaquette and photonic Harper–Hofstadter bands with quantum-Hall-like edge states.
registry.breaks: The synthetic potential is static and non-dynamical: there is no Lorentz force on a free photon and no gauge redundancy acting on matter. Pseudospin schemes keep time-reversal symmetry, so disorder that mixes pseudospins causes backscattering.
sources: Ozawa et al. (2019). "Topological photonics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 015006. [arXiv:1802.04173](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.04173)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Liénard–Wiechert = retarded Lorenz-gauge potentials
registry.summary: The Liénard–Wiechert potentials are the retarded solutions of the Lorenz-gauge wave equations for a point charge. The factor 1/(1−n·β), which comes from evaluating the delta function at retarded time, produces relativistic beaming and the γ^4 growth of synchrotron loss.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Magnetism as electrostatics plus relativity
registry.summary: In the rest frame of a charge moving beside a current-carrying wire, the magnetic force becomes an electric force from Lorentz-contracted, unbalanced line charges. The field-strength tensor makes E and B one object, and the field of a uniformly moving charge has B=v×E/c², which reduces to Biot–Savart at low speed.
registry.map: \mathbf E'_\perp=\gamma(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)_\perp,\quad \mathbf B=\frac{\mathbf v\times\mathbf E}{c^2}\ \text{(uniformly moving charge)}
registry.breaks: The derivation takes charge invariance and Lorentz covariance as inputs. Intrinsic magnetic moments (spin) do not come from moving charges.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Liénard's formula: the Lorentz-invariant Larmor power
registry.summary: Radiated power is a Lorentz scalar, so the non-relativistic Larmor formula fixes its covariant form in terms of the four-acceleration. This gives Liénard's γ^6 result and the γ^4/R^2 synchrotron loss, and aberration of the rest-frame dipole pattern gives the 1/γ beaming cone.
sources: Schwinger (1949). "On the Classical Radiation of Accelerated Electrons". *Phys. Rev.* 75, 1912. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.75.1912](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.75.1912)

registry.name: Localized plasmons: poles of the electrostatic sphere
registry.summary: The quasi-static sphere polarizability diverges at the Fröhlich condition ε_m(ω)=−2ε_d, which is the localized surface plasmon resonance of metal nanoparticles (ω_p/√3 for a Drude metal in vacuum). In the electrostatic limit Pendry's perfect lens needs only ε=−1, so Laplace-equation solutions are used to design near-field plasmonics.
registry.breaks: Loss (Im ε_m) caps the resonance. For particles beyond about λ/10, radiation damping and retardation red-shift and broaden it, and below about 2 nm nonlocal and quantum response shifts it.
sources: Pendry (2000). "Negative Refraction Makes a Perfect Lens". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 85, 3966. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966)

registry.name: Rayleigh scattering from the electrostatic dielectric sphere
registry.summary: A particle much smaller than λ sees a quasi-static field, so its induced dipole is that of a dielectric sphere in a uniform field, solved by Legendre separation of Laplace's equation. Radiating this dipole gives the ω^4 Rayleigh cross section with the same (ε−1)/(ε+2) factor.
registry.breaks: The quasi-static picture fails once ka or |m|ka is no longer small. Retardation, magnetic dipoles and higher multipoles then enter (the Mie regime).
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Designer ε(ω) and μ(ω) by homogenization
registry.summary: Metamaterials apply the macroscopic-field averaging of fields in matter (microscopic dipoles → P, M → ε, μ) to artificial sub-wavelength 'atoms'. Split rings give a resonant magnetization and wire arrays a Drude-like ε, so both can be made negative. Maxwell Garnett mixing is the Clausius–Mossotti relation applied to inclusions.
registry.breaks: Homogenization needs cells ≪λ. Real metamaterial cells are only λ/5–λ/10, so spatial dispersion, bianisotropy and loss leave ε and μ only approximately defined.
sources: Pendry (2000). "Negative Refraction Makes a Perfect Lens". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 85, 3966. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.3966)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Multipole expansion of radiating sources
registry.summary: The static multipole hierarchy carries over to time-harmonic sources: for ka≪1 the radiation field is a series of electric and magnetic multipoles, each order suppressed by about (ka)^2 relative to the one before, with electric-dipole radiation leading. The spherical harmonics of the static expansion become the vector spherical harmonics of the radiation pattern.
registry.map: \langle P_{E1}\rangle=\frac{\mu_0\omega^4|\mathbf p|^2}{12\pi c},\ P_{M1}:\ \mathbf p\to\mathbf m/c,\ P_{\ell+1}/P_\ell\sim(ka)^2

registry.name: Mie theory as a multipole expansion
registry.summary: Mie's exact solution for a sphere expands the scattered field in vector spherical harmonics: electric (a_n) and magnetic (b_n) multipoles of rising order. Rayleigh scattering is the leading electric-dipole term, and the number of multipoles needed grows with the size parameter x=ka.
sources: Mie (1908). "Beiträge zur Optik trüber Medien, speziell kolloidaler Metallösungen". *Ann. Phys.* 330, 377. [doi:10.1002/andp.19083300302](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19083300302)
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Free-electron lasers: stimulated undulator radiation
registry.summary: An FEL turns the spontaneous undulator radiation of relativistic electrons into laser light. The ponderomotive coupling between the beam and the co-propagating field microbunches the electrons at the resonant wavelength, so emission becomes coherent and grows exponentially without population inversion of bound states.
registry.breaks: The gain is a collective classical bunching instability, not inversion between discrete levels. SASE output starts from shot noise and has poor temporal coherence unless seeded.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Inhibited and enhanced emission: dipoles in engineered LDOS
registry.summary: The power a dipole radiates depends on its surroundings through the local density of states, i.e. the imaginary part of the Green's function at the source. Photonic band gaps suppress emission (Yablonovitch), while cavities and plasmonic nanoantennas enhance it (Purcell). A radio antenna's radiation resistance shifts near reflectors for the same reason.
registry.map: \frac{P}{P_0}=\frac{6\pi c}{\omega}\hat{\mathbf p}\cdot\mathrm{Im}\,\mathbf G(\mathbf r_0,\mathbf r_0)\cdot\hat{\mathbf p},\quad F_P=\frac{3}{4\pi^2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^3\frac{Q}{V}

registry.name: Stimulated Raman and Brillouin scattering
registry.summary: Spontaneous Raman scattering (molecular vibrations) and Brillouin scattering (acoustic phonons) turn stimulated at high intensity. The pump–Stokes beat drives the material excitation coherently, giving exponential Stokes gain through the imaginary part of the resonant χ(3). SBS limits the power of narrow-linewidth fibre lasers.
registry.review: interim: not yet reviewed by a specialist

registry.name: Coherent backscattering is weak localization
registry.summary: In a disordered medium each multiple-scattering path interferes constructively with its time-reversed partner in the exact backward direction, doubling the reflected intensity in a cone of width ~λ/ℓ*; this is the optical twin of the weak-localization correction to electrical conductance and a precursor of Anderson localization.
sources: Wolf & Maret (1985). "Weak Localization and Coherent Backscattering of Photons in Disordered Media". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 55, 2696. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2696](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2696)

van Albada & Lagendijk (1985). "Observation of Weak Localization of Light in a Random Medium". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 55, 2692. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2692](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.55.2692)

registry.name: Thermal light: Bose–Einstein fluctuations and bunching
registry.summary: A single mode of thermal light has a geometric Bose–Einstein photon-number distribution with variance n̄ + n̄². The n̄² wave term is classical interference of random phasors (Gaussian statistics, g⁽²⁾(0) = 2, Hanbury Brown–Twiss bunching); the n̄ term is particle shot noise. Together they are Einstein's 1909 fluctuation formula for blackbody radiation.

registry.name: Wiener–Khinchin: spectra from correlation functions
registry.summary: The optical power spectrum is the Fourier transform of the field autocorrelation (Wiener–Khinchin), the same relation that defines noise spectral densities in linear-response theory; the FDT then ties the spectrum of thermal light to the absorptive response of the emitter.

registry.name: Speckle as a random walk of phasors
registry.summary: A speckle field is a sum of many phasors with random phases, a two-dimensional random walk, so by the central limit theorem it is a circular Gaussian field with exponential intensity statistics and unit contrast. Pearson posed the random-walk problem in 1905 and Rayleigh answered it from his theory of superposed vibrations of random phase.

registry.name: Maximum-entropy image reconstruction
registry.summary: Reconstructing an image from incomplete Fourier data (interferometer visibilities, blurred noisy images) is underdetermined; choosing the image of maximum entropy consistent with the data within the noise is Jaynes's MaxEnt inference transplanted to imaging, a standard deconvolution method in radio astronomy.

registry.name: Étendue conservation and the brightness theorem
registry.summary: Étendue n²A dΩ is the phase-space volume of a ray bundle and is conserved by any passive optical system (Liouville), so radiance cannot be increased and no lens or mirror can heat a target above the Sun's surface temperature; this is the second law in ray optics and fixes the maximum solar concentration n²/sin²θ_s.

registry.name: Cavity mode counting and the Planck law
registry.summary: The density of electromagnetic standing-wave modes in a cavity, 8πν²/c³, times the mean energy per mode gives the blackbody spectrum: equipartition (k_BT per mode) yields Rayleigh–Jeans and the ultraviolet catastrophe, while Bose–Einstein occupation of each mode as a quantum oscillator yields Planck's law.
registry.breaks: Weyl mode counting needs cavity size ≫ λ; in sub-wavelength cavities and photonic crystals the density of states is engineered and the free-space Planck law no longer applies.

registry.name: Johnson–Nyquist noise from a 1D blackbody line
registry.summary: Nyquist derived thermal voltage noise by letting two resistors exchange energy through a lossless transmission line whose modes each hold k_BT, a one-dimensional blackbody; this is the first fluctuation–dissipation theorem, generalized by Callen–Welton. The same physics sets antenna noise temperature, which is how the CMB was first read.

registry.name: Radiation pressure and the Stefan–Boltzmann law
registry.summary: The Maxwell stress tensor gives isotropic radiation the pressure p = u/3; inserting this into the thermodynamic identity (∂U/∂V)_T = T(∂p/∂T)_V − p forces u ∝ T⁴ (Boltzmann 1884), and the adiabatic invariant VT³ = const gives Wien's displacement law.

registry.name: Bohr–van Leeuwen theorem: no classical magnetism
registry.summary: With minimal coupling H(p − qA), the classical canonical partition function is independent of A after shifting the momentum integration, so classical statistical mechanics predicts zero equilibrium magnetization; diamagnetism and paramagnetism are quantum effects. Gauge invariance of the partition function is the formal content.

registry.name: Poisson–Boltzmann and Debye–Hückel as mean-field electrostatics
registry.summary: Closing Poisson's equation with Boltzmann-distributed ion densities gives the Poisson–Boltzmann equation, a mean-field theory of electrolytes and charged colloids; linearized it yields Debye–Hückel screening, and it fails (ion correlations, like-charge attraction) exactly where fluctuations beyond mean field matter.

registry.name: Magnetocaloric effect and adiabatic demagnetization
registry.summary: Adding the field work term μ₀H·dM (or E·dP) to the fundamental relation makes H and M a conjugate pair like −p and V; the resulting Maxwell relation gives the magnetocaloric and electrocaloric effects and adiabatic demagnetization, the classic route to millikelvin temperatures.

registry.name: Effective-medium theory and percolating composites
registry.summary: The effective permittivity or conductivity of a metal–dielectric composite (Maxwell Garnett, Bruggeman) is a mean-field theory of a random network; Bruggeman's symmetric theory predicts a conductor–insulator threshold (p_c = 1/3 in 3D), and near the true percolation threshold metal films show power-law conductivity and giant local-field fluctuations.

registry.name: Langevin–Debye orientational polarizability
registry.summary: Permanent dipoles in a field have canonical weights e^{pE cosθ/k_BT}; averaging gives the Langevin function and, at weak field, the Debye orientational polarizability p²/3k_BT, the electric twin of Curie's law for paramagnets and the microscopic origin of temperature-dependent ε and χ.

registry.name: Dielectric function as a causal response function
registry.summary: ε(ω) and the Drude/Lorentz models are the archetypal linear-response functions: causality makes χ analytic in the upper half-plane, giving the Kramers–Kronig relations between refraction and absorption; Im ε measures dissipation, and Kubo's formula gives the optical conductivity from equilibrium current correlations.

registry.name: Landau–Devonshire theory of ferroelectrics

registry.name: Shannon capacity limits of optical fibre
registry.summary: Shannon's channel capacity bounds data rates in fibre networks; because Kerr nonlinearity makes noise grow with launch power, achievable spectral efficiency peaks at an optimum power (the nonlinear Shannon limit), tying information entropy to fibre physics.

registry.name: Chemical potential of light: photon BEC versus lasing
registry.summary: When photons thermalize by repeated absorption and re-emission in a dye-filled microcavity, their number is conserved and they acquire a chemical potential; above a critical number they Bose-condense into the lowest cavity mode, distinct from lasing, which needs inversion. registry.name: Random and multimode lasers as photonic spin glasses
registry.summary: Mode amplitudes of multimode lasers evolve under an effective Hamiltonian of four-mode couplings; with random couplings (random lasers) this is a spherical p-spin glass at an effective temperature set by noise over pump squared, and replica-symmetry breaking has been reported in shot-to-shot spectral fluctuations. Passive mode-locking is the ordered phase of the same theory.

registry.summary: Spontaneous emission kicks the laser phase randomly; above threshold the amplitude is pinned but the phase performs Brownian motion, so the field correlation decays exponentially and the line is a Lorentzian of Schawlow–Townes width, the Langevin/Fokker–Planck laser theory of Lax and Haken.

registry.name: Laser threshold as a second-order phase transition
registry.summary: Near threshold the single-mode laser field obeys a Langevin equation with a Landau-type potential whose quadratic coefficient changes sign with pump: the field amplitude is an order parameter with mean-field exponent β = 1/2, spontaneous emission is the noise, and the free phase behaves like a Goldstone mode.

registry.name: Anderson localization of light
registry.summary: Anderson localization is a wave-interference effect, so it applies to light: John proposed strong photon localization near the band edges of disordered photonic crystals, and transverse localization has been imaged in disordered photonic lattices. registry.name: Atom interferometry: optical interferometers for atoms
registry.summary: Light-pulse atom interferometers copy the Mach–Zehnder geometry, with laser pulses as beam splitters and mirrors, and Ramsey's separated-field method is a two-slit experiment in time. They measure g, rotations and h/m and test the equivalence principle.

registry.name: Huygens–Fresnel principle as free-particle propagator
registry.summary: Fresnel diffraction sums secondary wavelets weighted by e^{ikr}, just as Feynman's path integral sums e^{iS/ħ}. The paraxial Fresnel kernel is the free-particle propagator with z↔t and k↔m/ħ, and stationary phase picks out rays, the optical counterpart of classical paths.

registry.name: Beam splitters: Mach–Zehnder to Hong–Ou–Mandel
registry.summary: The beam-splitter unitary is the same for classical field amplitudes and for photon creation operators, so a single photon reproduces classical fringes. registry.summary: Circularly polarized light carries spin angular momentum ±ħ per photon (Beth 1936), and Laguerre–Gauss beams with phase e^{iℓφ} carry orbital angular momentum ℓħ. Transfer to atoms follows the Δm selection rules, and both degrees of freedom serve as qudit encodings.

registry.summary: Pancharatnam (1956) found that light taken around a closed cycle of polarization states gains a phase of minus half the solid angle it encloses on the Poincaré sphere. registry.summary: The 2×2 coherency matrix of partially polarized light is a density matrix whose Stokes parameters are the Bloch-vector components. The degree of polarization is the Bloch-vector length, wave plates act as unitaries, and depolarizing elements (Mueller matrices) act as quantum channels.

registry.summary: Below the cutoff of the second vertical mode, a flat microwave cavity's TM modes obey the 2D Helmholtz equation, which is the Schrödinger equation of a particle in a hard-wall billiard. Measured resonance spectra test random-matrix level statistics (GOE for chaotic shapes) and wavefunction scarring.
